Use $\mathbb N$ from [[def-natural-numbers]], which includes $0$, and define $\mathbb N_{>0}:=\mathbb N\setminus\{0\}$. A **finite-state thermodynamic-limit contract** specifies a sequence $(X_k,E_k,g_k,V_k,n_k)_{k\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$, where each $X_k$ is a finite nonempty state set, $E_k:X_k\to\mathbb R$ assigns finite energies in joules, $g_k:X_k\to(0,\infty)$ assigns positive dimensionless weights, $V_k>0$ is physical volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, and, for one declared species, $n_k>0$ is its amount in moles. A fixed-density sequence has $V_k\to\infty$ and $n_k/V_k\to\rho\in(0,\infty)$ in $\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}$. Boundary conditions, interaction rules, and the choice of a volume or amount normalization are part of the contract and must be held fixed or explicitly tracked as $k$ varies.

For $T>0$, set $\beta:=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$, with $k_B$ and units from [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The finite-state canonical partition sum is

$$
Z_k(\beta):=\sum_{x\in X_k}g_k(x)e^{-\beta E_k(x)},
$$

as the finite case of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. It is a positive finite real number. Define $F_k(\beta):=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k(\beta)$ in joules and $f_k(\beta):=F_k(\beta)/V_k$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. The specified thermodynamic-limit value is $f(\beta,\rho):=\lim_{k\to\infty} f_k(\beta)$ **if this limit exists**. A limit per mole or per lattice site is a different normalization and must be stated separately.

This is a contract for what a limit claim must specify, not a theorem that the limit exists. It asserts no uniformity in $\beta$, derivative interchange, ensemble equivalence, convergence rate, or nonanalyticity. A finite model's regularity and any limiting singularity require their own arguments; neither is inferred from the word “thermodynamic limit.”

statement.before:
Fix a closed system $s$ of constitution $c$, with equilibrium domain $D_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], and fix $T_0>0$ and $p_0>0$. Define, for $x\in D_c$,
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x):=U_c(x)+p_0V_c(x)-T_0S_c(x),
$$
where $U_c,V_c$ are the dimensioned energy and volume maps of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and $S_c$ is the adopted entropy of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Thus $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ has units joules.

Let $P_s\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ be an admitted closed system process record as defined in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]], with system endpoints $x_{P_s}^-,x_{P_s}^+\in D_c$. Let $R$ be its ideal thermal reservoir and $B$ its ideal pressure store; both lie inside a declared isolated-compound outer boundary. Let $\widehat P$ be an admitted process record for that isolated compound. By an extension, require that $\widehat P$ has the same time interval, system endpoints, system configuration path, and system-side protocol and transfer records as $P_s$, together with the reservoir and store records. Write its compound endpoint association as
$$
\rho_{\widehat P}(\pm)=(x_{P_s}^\pm,y_R^\pm,y_B^\pm)\in\mathcal F\subseteq D_c\times Y_R\times Y_B,
$$
where $Y_R,Y_B$ are the model-declared reservoir and store state sets and $\mathcal F$ is the exact feasible endpoint set from [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The system protocol assigns heat $Q[P_s]$ and work $W_{\rm on}[P_s]$ to $P_s$; the auxiliary endpoint changes in $\widehat P$ satisfy the reservoir and store relations in [A1]–[A2] below. No matter crosses the compound boundary, no work channel other than pressure-store work acts on the system, and no other energy-coordinate changes are omitted.

Then the system endpoint difference obeys
$$
\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^+)-\Phi_{T_0,p_0}(x_{P_s}^-)\le0.
$$
If the final compound endpoint $\rho_{\widehat P}(+)$ is an attained global entropy maximum on $\mathcal F$, then $x_{P_s}^+$ attains a global minimum of $\Phi_{T_0,p_0}$ on the system projection
$$
\Pi_s(\mathcal F):=\{x\in D_c:\exists y_R\in Y_R,\ y_B\in Y_B\text{ with }(x,y_R,y_B)\in\mathcal F\}.
$$
This is a conditional model deduction; it does not assert that arbitrary fixed-$T,p$ reactions have this preparation or that the system reaches the minimum dynamically.

Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]] give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of [[def-finite-sum]]. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]]. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in [[def-td-response-functions]] and [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], on the exact feasible set of [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in [[post-td-entropy-maximum]]. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

statement.before:
Fix $C\ge1$ species and $R\ge1$ declared internal reaction extents. Let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{C\times R}$ be the dimensionless stoichiometric matrix, let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^C$ have units mol, and let $\xi\in\mathbb R^R$ have units mol. The amount vector is $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$, and the nonnegative-amount feasible extent set is
$$
\mathcal F_\nu:=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^R:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^C\}.
$$
Assume the exact local reaction-feasible extent set is $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$; no additional local constraint removes any direction in its tangent cone.
Fix $T_0>0$ and $p_0>0$ in a declared natural-variable chart. On an open neighborhood $U$ of a candidate endpoint $\xi_*$, let $\Phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be a finite $C^1$ constrained Gibbs-potential extension, in joules, satisfying
$$
D\Phi(\xi)[h]=\sum_{j=1}^C\mu_j(\xi)(\nu h)_j=(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi))\cdot h,
$$
where every $\mu_j$ is in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. At positive amounts, require $\Phi(\xi)=U_c(x(\xi))+p_0V_c(x(\xi))-T_0S_c(x(\xi))$ for the system state $x(\xi)$, with $U_c,V_c,S_c$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]] and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]; its derivative is that of the local Gibbs chart supplied by [[def-td-legendre-potentials]] and [[pthm-td-potential-differentials]].

If all amounts at $\xi_*$ are positive, assume $\xi_*$ is the system endpoint of a closed system process record and its admitted isolated-compound extension exactly as in [[pthm-td-fixed-tp-reaction-potential-minimum]], is a global entropy-maximizing endpoint on that extension's exact feasible set, and the record's system projection contains every state $x(\xi)$ for $\xi\in\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$. If at least one amount is zero, it is outside [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]; in that boundary case, assume instead that the model supplies a boundary-inclusive state domain with finite $C^1$ maps $\bar U_c,\bar V_c,\bar S_c:U\to\mathbb R$ in joules, $\mathrm{m^3}$, and $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, respectively, that $\Phi(\xi)=\bar U_c(\xi)+p_0\bar V_c(\xi)-T_0\bar S_c(\xi)$, and that its exact isolated-compound model has fixed total energy, an ideal reservoir with $S_R(E_R)=S_{R,0}+E_R/T_0$, a constant-entropy pressure store satisfying $E_B-p_0\bar V_c(\xi)=C_B$, and a feasible-set projection equal to $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$. Assume $\xi_*$ is an attained global entropy maximum on that boundary-inclusive set. This additional boundary model premise is not supplied by the positive-mole state chart or by [[pthm-td-fixed-tp-reaction-potential-minimum]].

Under the relevant interior or boundary assumptions above, $\xi_*$ locally minimizes $\Phi$ on $\mathcal F_\nu\cap U$. Let $J_*:=\{j:n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j=0\}$ be the active species set. Then the first-order necessary condition is
$$
(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi_*))\cdot h\ge0\qquad\text{for every }h\in T_{\mathcal F_\nu}(\xi_*),
$$
where
$$
T_{\mathcal F_\nu}(\xi_*):=\{h\in\mathbb R^R:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J_*\}.
$$
If $\xi_*$ is interior to $\mathcal F_\nu$, this reduces to $\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu(\xi_*)=0$. If, in addition, $\Phi$ is convex and differentiable on a convex neighborhood containing the relevant feasible set, the same tangent inequality is sufficient for global minimization there.

Let $\alpha,\beta$ be two one-component phase branches from [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] on a common open chart $O\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(T,p)$. Assume each branch has a local $C^2$ energy representation $\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)$, $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, and that within each fixed branch tag it satisfies the same-tag homogeneity
$$
\mathcal U_i(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n)=\lambda\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)
$$
for all $\lambda$ in a neighborhood of $1$ for which the scaled state remains in the chart. This is a phase-branch hypothesis: the general tagged law of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] does not imply it. It may be stipulated independently on each local branch, or supplied by the common-law bulk subclass of [[pthm-td-euler-and-gibbs-duhem]] when each phase's local inverse states lie in its designated entropy cone with fixed species and intensive parameters and common SI units and energy/entropy reference conventions. That supplied subclass uses local inverse uniqueness and does not require a global energy inverse.

Suppose a state $(T_0,p_0)\in O$ is an attained interior coexistence equilibrium with bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange between the two branches, and both branches admit the valid local Gibbs charts of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Write $g_i=G_i/n_i$, $s_i=S_i/n_i$, and $v_i=V_i/n_i$ in the units specified by [[def-td-si-quantities]]. If
$$
\Delta v(T_0,p_0):=v_\beta(T_0,p_0)-v_\alpha(T_0,p_0)\ne0,
$$
then, on some open interval about $T_0$, the equal-Gibbs-per-mole coexistence condition $g_\alpha(T,p(T))=g_\beta(T,p(T))$ defines a unique local $C^1$ curve and
$$
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
$$
If, in addition, conversion from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ is admitted as a reversible process in contact with an ideal thermal reservoir at the same fixed $T$, and the full finite isolated compound (converted phases, reservoir, work stores and all auxiliaries) has equilibrium endpoints with additive component entropy, with every component other than the converted phases and that reservoir having zero entropy change, and the admitted forward and reverse complete-compound records have nonnegative total endpoint entropy changes for that same additive split with their full endpoint tuples interchanged, then its molar latent heat absorbed by the system is $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. Assume each branch has a local $C^2$ energy representation $\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)$, $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, and that within each fixed branch tag it satisfies the same-tag homogeneity
$$
\mathcal U_i(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n)=\lambda\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)
$$
for all $\lambda$ in a neighborhood of $1$ for which the scaled state remains in the chart. This is a phase-branch hypothesis: the general tagged law of *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling* does not imply it. It may be stipulated independently on each local branch, or supplied by the common-law bulk subclass of *Euler and Gibbs-Duhem identities under same-tag homogeneity* when each phase's local inverse states lie in its designated entropy cone with fixed species and intensive parameters and common SI units and energy/entropy reference conventions. That supplied subclass uses local inverse uniqueness and does not require a global energy inverse.

Suppose a state $(T_0,p_0)\in O$ is an attained interior coexistence equilibrium with bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange between the two branches, and both branches admit the valid local Gibbs charts of *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials*. Write $g_i=G_i/n_i$, $s_i=S_i/n_i$, and $v_i=V_i/n_i$ in the units specified by *SI quantities and unit conventions*. If
$$
\Delta v(T_0,p_0):=v_\beta(T_0,p_0)-v_\alpha(T_0,p_0)\ne0,
$$
then, on some open interval about $T_0$, the equal-Gibbs-per-mole coexistence condition $g_\alpha(T,p(T))=g_\beta(T,p(T))$ defines a unique local $C^1$ curve and
$$
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
$$
If, in addition, conversion from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ is admitted as a reversible process in contact with an ideal thermal reservoir at the same fixed $T$, and the full finite isolated compound (converted phases, reservoir, work stores and all auxiliaries) has equilibrium endpoints with additive component entropy, with every component other than the converted phases and that reservoir having zero entropy change, and the admitted forward and reverse complete-compound records have nonnegative total endpoint entropy changes for that same additive split with their full endpoint tuples interchanged, then its molar latent heat absorbed by the system is $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. Let $C\ge1$ be the number of named species, $P\ge1$ the number of coexisting phase branches, and $R\ge0$ the number of independent internal reaction directions. Let each branch chemical-potential map
$$

$$
be $C^1$ on a common open domain
$$
\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times(\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ})^P \subseteq\mathbb R^{\,n},\qquad n=2+P(C-1).
$$
Let $\nu^1,\ldots,\nu^R\in\mathbb R^C$ be linearly independent, dimensionless stoichiometric vectors, with extents measured in moles. Assume that, for every phase pair and each of energy, volume, and every named species, the feasible set contains the pairwise transfer curve for all sufficiently small transfers of either sign, varying only the selected coordinate in those two phases with opposite increments and holding every other state coordinate of both phases, all other phases, and all auxiliaries fixed. For each phase $\alpha$ and reaction $r$, assume the feasible set contains the complete endpoint curve with species amounts $n^\alpha(t)=n^{\alpha,*}+t\nu^r$ for all sufficiently small extents $t$ of either sign, while that phase's energy and volume, all other reaction extents, and every other phase's state remain fixed at their coexistence values. Require the total entropy contribution of all retained auxiliaries along each such reaction curve to be differentiable at zero extent with derivative zero. Every auxiliary state may be fixed as a sufficient special case, but entropy-neutral varying auxiliary or work-device states are permitted. Phase equilibrium imposes $\mu_i^\alpha-\mu_i^1=0$ for $1\le i\le C$, $2\le\alpha\le P$; internal reaction equilibrium imposes $(\nu^r)^{\mathsf T}\mu^\alpha=0$ in every phase for $1\le r\le R$. On the phase-equality locus these are the same $R$ equations in each phase, so count them once using phase 1. Put $q:=C(P-1)$ and $m:=q+R$. If $m=0$ (equivalently $P=1,R=0$), no equation is imposed and the local zero set is the whole chart, of dimension $n=C+1=C-P+2-R$. $$
n-q-R=C-P+2-R.
$$
This is the dimension of the equation zero set in intensive coordinates only; phase amounts and their extensive conservation constraints are not counted, and the actual stable-coexistence set may be a proper subset after additional stability constraints. If the nonsingular-minor condition fails, no dimension formula is asserted.

statement.proposed:
Fix $d\ge1$, the site set $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, its max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$, and the local spin algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of the uniformly finite-dimensional spin system. A finite interaction is a family $\Phi(Z)=\Phi(Z)^*\in\mathcal A_Z$ indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define

$$H_\Lambda^\Phi:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z),\qquad \tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar},$$

where $\hbar>0$, $A$ is embedded in a common finite local algebra, and the finite sum is a self-adjoint matrix. When a path $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, is used, each $\Phi_s(Z)$ is $C^1$ in matrix norm and the derivative is taken term by term.

For $r\ge0$ put $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$. The admissible weights used here are

$$F_a(r):=e^{-ar}F(r)\quad(a>0),\qquad F_\rho(r):=(1+r)^{-\rho}\quad(\rho>d).$$

For an admissible weight $G$, define the weighted interaction norm

$$\|\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma}\frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{\substack{Z\subset\Gamma\ {\rm finite,\ nonempty}\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Phi(Z)\|.$$

The derivative norm of a path is

$$\|\partial\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{Z\ni x,y}|Z|\,\|\partial_s\Phi_s(Z)\|.$$

A finite-volume spectral band is a nonempty selected subset $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\subseteq\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})$ together with the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. It may be specified by an interval $I_\Lambda(s)$ with smoothly varying endpoints, in which case $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)=\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\cap I_\Lambda(s)$. The band is uniformly isolated with gap $\gamma>0$ along a specified finite-volume exhaustion when

$$\operatorname{dist}\!\left(\Sigma_\Lambda(s),\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\setminus\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\right)\ge\gamma$$

for every volume in that exhaustion and every $s\in[0,1]$. For spectral-flow arguments, the selected eigenvalues must also form a locally fixed spectral cluster: for each $s_0$, a contour in the resolvent set encloses exactly the selected eigenvalues for all $s$ in a neighborhood of $s_0$. In finite dimension this implies that its projection is $C^1$ when the Hamiltonian path is $C^1$. This cluster condition holds, for example, for the first $r_\Lambda$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity when the integer $r_\Lambda$ is fixed along the path and the gap after them stays open. Uniform distance between the selected and unselected spectra alone does not prevent an interval from changing membership discontinuously. A ground band is such a band containing the lowest eigenvalue or a finite-volume cluster of lowest eigenvalues; no uniqueness is implicit.

For physical units, take interaction terms and Hamiltonians in joules, time in seconds, and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds. The path parameter $s$, lattice distance, and admissible weights are dimensionless; the interaction norm therefore has energy units and the derivative norm has energy units per dimensionless path parameter.

Let $X,Y\subset\mathbb Z^d$ be finite regions and $A\in\mathcal A_Y$. Embed $A$ in $\mathcal A_{X\cup Y}$, use the canonical site-order permutation to group factors in $X\cap Y$ and $Y\setminus X$, and apply the normalized trace on the omitted factors:

$$E_X(A):=\bigl(\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A_{X\cap Y}}\otimes \tau_{Y\setminus X}\bigr)(A)\otimes I_{X\setminus Y}\in\mathcal A_X,\qquad \tau_D:=q^{-|D|}\operatorname{Tr}_D.$$

The empty tensor factor has normalized trace $1$. Since $\tau_D(I_D)=1$, adding an identity factor does not change the result, so this formula consistently defines $E_X$ on the directed union $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$. This definition alone asserts no norm extension to its completion.

Let $G$ be a finite group with identity $e$, and let $\Sigma$ be a finite oriented cellulation of a closed connected surface. Write $V,E,F$ for its vertex, edge, and face sets. Each edge $a\in E$ has a chosen source $s(a)$ and target $t(a)$. For a configuration $\mathbf g=(g_a)_{a\in E}\in G^E$, the edge Hilbert space is $\mathcal H_\Sigma=\bigotimes_{a\in E}\mathbb C[G]$, with orthonormal configuration basis $|\mathbf g\rangle$.

For $v\in V$ and $x\in G$, put $k_u=x$ if $u=v$ and $k_u=e$ otherwise. Define the vertex gauge permutation $U_v(x)$ on basis vectors by

$$U_v(x)|\mathbf g\rangle=|\mathbf g'\rangle,\qquad g'_a=k_{s(a)}g_a k_{t(a)}^{-1}\quad(a\in E).$$

For a face $f\in F$, choose its oriented boundary walk $a_1^{\epsilon_1}\cdots a_m^{\epsilon_m}$, with $\epsilon_j=1$ when the walk follows the selected orientation of edge $a_j$ and $\epsilon_j=-1$ otherwise. Its based holonomy on $\mathbf g$ is

$$H_f(\mathbf g):=g_{a_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots g_{a_m}^{\epsilon_m}.$$

Define the vertex average, face flatness projector, and finite lattice Hamiltonian by

$$A_v:=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{x\in G}U_v(x),\qquad B_f|\mathbf g\rangle:=\mathbf 1_{H_f(\mathbf g)=e}|\mathbf g\rangle,\qquad H_\Sigma:=\sum_{v\in V}(I-A_v)+\sum_{f\in F}(I-B_f).$$
statement.proposed:
Let $G$ be a finite group with identity $e$. A **closed connected surface** means a compact, connected topological $2$-manifold without boundary. A **finite cellulation** here is a finite decomposition of such a surface into vertices, edges, and faces, where each face interior is an open disk and its attaching boundary is a finite cyclic walk along edges. An **oriented** cellulation means that each edge has a chosen direction, recorded by its source and target; no orientation of the surface is assumed. Let $\Sigma$ be such a cellulation and write $V,E,F$ for its vertex, edge, and face sets. Each edge $a\in E$ has source $s(a)$ and target $t(a)$. For a configuration $\mathbf g=(g_a)_{a\in E}\in G^E$, the edge Hilbert space is $\mathcal H_\Sigma=\bigotimes_{a\in E}\mathbb C[G]$, with orthonormal configuration basis $|\mathbf g\rangle$.

For $v\in V$ and $x\in G$, put $k_u=x$ if $u=v$ and $k_u=e$ otherwise. Define the vertex gauge permutation $U_v(x)$ on basis vectors by

$$U_v(x)|\mathbf g\rangle=|\mathbf g'\rangle,\qquad g'_a=k_{s(a)}g_a k_{t(a)}^{-1}\quad(a\in E).$$

For a face $f\in F$, choose its oriented boundary walk $a_1^{\epsilon_1}\cdots a_m^{\epsilon_m}$, with $\epsilon_j=1$ when the walk follows the selected orientation of edge $a_j$ and $\epsilon_j=-1$ otherwise. Its based holonomy on $\mathbf g$ is

$$H_f(\mathbf g):=g_{a_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots g_{a_m}^{\epsilon_m}.$$

Define the vertex average, face flatness projector, and finite lattice Hamiltonian by

$$A_v:=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{x\in G}U_v(x),\qquad B_f|\mathbf g\rangle:=\mathbf 1_{H_f(\mathbf g)=e}|\mathbf g\rangle,\qquad H_\Sigma:=\sum_{v\in V}(I-A_v)+\sum_{f\in F}(I-B_f).$$

statement.before: Let $G$ be a finite group and let $\Sigma$ be a finite oriented cellulation of a closed connected surface, with vertex gauge permutations $U_v(x)$, vertex averages $A_v$, face flatness projectors $B_f$, and Hamiltonian $H_\Sigma$ defined using the group-element edge basis and oriented boundary holonomies. Then all $A_v$ and $B_f$ are commuting orthogonal projections. The Hamiltonian $H_\Sigma$ is positive and has a nonzero common zero vector for all terms $I-A_v$ and $I-B_f$; hence the finite model is frustration-free with ground energy zero.

statement.proposed:
Let $N\geq1$ and let $\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$ have the standard tensor-product Hermitian inner product, linear in its first argument, with $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ orthonormal on each factor. For $1\leq i<N$, let $s_i$ be the swap of tensor factors $i,i+1$, let $|\omega\rangle=(|01\rangle-|10\rangle)/\sqrt2$, and let $P_i=I^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes|\omega\rangle\langle\omega|\otimes I^{\otimes(N-i-1)}$ be the projection onto this singlet on those two factors. Put $e_i:=I-s_i$. Then these are the loop-weight-two Temperley-Lieb generators. In the Hecke normalization $g_i(q):=qI-e_i$, at $q=1$ one has $g_i(1)=s_i$. For arbitrary real coefficients $\mathcal J_i$, the finite exchange sum
$$X_N(\boldsymbol{\mathcal J}):=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\mathcal J_i s_i$$
satisfies
$$X_N(\boldsymbol{\mathcal J})=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\mathcal J_i\right)I-\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\mathcal J_i e_i.$$
The equality $g_i(1)=s_i$ is internal to this spin-half representation; it does not identify its state space with the distinct $Q=4$ Potts representation.

statement.before:
Fix one section $\Sigma$, one declared scheme, and one regulator-label sequence $(\Lambda_n)_{n\ge1}$. For each $r\in\{0,1\}$, take $H_{\mathrm{in},n}=\mathbb C$ and $H_{\mathrm{out},n}=\mathbb C^2$ with their standard inner products and bases $(1)$ and $(f_0,f_1)$. In the ordered product basis $(1\otimes f_0,1\otimes f_1)$, use the joint density matrices $\rho_n^{(0)}=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/2)$ and $\rho_n^{(1)}=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ for every $n\ge1$. Use the same finite geometric value $S_{\mathrm{grav},n}[\Sigma]=G$ for both sequences and all $n$, where $G$ is a fixed finite real value with units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The index $r$ labels these two sequences only; it is neither physical time nor regulator order. Define $S_{\mathrm{gen}}^{\mathrm{ren},r}[\Sigma]:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\bigl(S_{\mathrm{grav},n}[\Sigma]+S_{\mathrm{out},n}^{(r)}\bigr)$. These limits exist and satisfy

$$S_{\mathrm{gen}}^{\mathrm{ren},1}[\Sigma]-S_{\mathrm{gen}}^{\mathrm{ren},0}[\Sigma]=-k_B\log 2<0.$$

The fixed-section definition supplies no ordered parameter set $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, cut family $s\mapsto\Sigma_s$, state family $s\mapsto(\rho_{s,n})_{n\ge1}$, or comparison inequality such as $S_{\mathrm{gen}}^{\mathrm{ren}}[\Sigma_{s_2}]\ge S_{\mathrm{gen}}^{\mathrm{ren}}[\Sigma_{s_1}]$ for $s_1\le s_2$ in $J$. The displayed comparison is between independently specified model-data sequences, not a physical evolution. The restricted classical area-increase result and the restricted area-entropy calibration result do not supply an inequality for the outside-state entropy.
statement.proposed: The calculation compares two independent sequences of model data at one fixed section. A monotonicity claim for a specified family of cuts would require an ordered parameter set $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a section $\Sigma_s$ and a regulator/state/geometric sequence at each $s\in J$, finite convergence at each $s$ if renormalized values are used, and a proof that $S_{\mathrm{gen}}^{\mathrm{ren}}[\Sigma_{s_2}]\ge S_{\mathrm{gen}}^{\mathrm{ren}}[\Sigma_{s_1}]$ whenever $s_1\le s_2$ in $J$. None of this comparison data or inequality is part of the fixed-section definition or supplied by the finite example.

statement.before: For a fixed generator and bifurcation surface, with the canonical covariant first-variation potential and Noether charge representative and vanishing residual-constraint variation, delta integral_B Q_xi = (hbar kappa/(2 pi k_B)) delta S_W, where S_W=-(2 pi k_B/hbar) integral_B P^(abcd) epsilon_ab epsilon_cd dA_B.
statement.proposed:
Use the stationary Noether data of the preceding Definition, with fixed $\xi$, compact boundaryless bifurcation surface $B$, and surface gravity $\kappa>0$. Choose the covariant first-variation potential and $Q_\xi$ in the canonical local representative class of the preceding Noether-charge decomposition theorem. Let $\nabla$ be the Levi-Civita connection of $g$, use the curvature convention
$$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z,$$
and write $R_{abcd}:=g(R(e_c,e_d)e_b,e_a)$ in any local frame and $R:=g^{ac}g^{bd}R_{abcd}$. Write $\mathcal L=\ell(g,\psi,\nabla\psi,\ldots,R)\,\boldsymbol\epsilon_g$, where $\boldsymbol\epsilon_g$ is the oriented metric volume form and $\ell$ depends smoothly on the Riemann tensor algebraically, with no covariant derivatives of $R$. Define $P^{abcd}$ to be the Riemann-symmetric metric representative of the differential of $\ell$ in its curvature argument:
$$\delta\ell\big|_{g,\psi,\nabla\psi,\ldots}=P^{abcd}\delta R_{abcd}.$$
Here $P$ satisfies $P^{abcd}=-P^{bacd}=-P^{abdc}=P^{cdab}$ and $P^{a[bcd]}=0$. Let $dA_B$ be the positive volume form of the induced Riemannian metric on $B$ (in local coordinates with induced metric $h$, $dA_B=\sqrt{\det h}\,dy^1\cdots dy^{n-2}$), and define the stationary Wald Noether-charge functional
$$S_W:=-\frac{2\pi k_B}{\hbar}\int_B P^{abcd}\epsilon_{ab}\epsilon_{cd}\,dA_B.$$
For every admitted smooth linearized perturbation at the stationary solution, with $\xi$ and $B$ fixed and the residual constraint variation $\delta C_\xi=0$, the chosen Noether charge satisfies
$$\delta\int_B Q_\xi=\frac{\hbar\kappa}{2\pi k_B}\,\delta S_W.$$
Here $\hbar>0$ is Planck's constant, $k_B>0$ is Boltzmann's constant, and the action normalization is $c=1$. The identity is evaluated at the unperturbed value of $\kappa$; it does not include a $\delta\kappa$ term.

statement.before: For finite hypersurface chains with boundary S_R-B, the stated constraint, and an integrable asymptotic Hamiltonian variation, delta H_xi equals the bifurcation-surface charge variation and hence (hbar kappa/(2 pi k_B)) delta S_W. Einstein-Hilbert gives S_W=k_B A_B/(4G hbar) for c=1.
statement.proposed:
For the stationary Noether data of the preceding Definition, choose $Q_\xi$ in the canonical local representative class of the preceding Noether-charge decomposition theorem. Let $\delta\phi$ be an admitted linearized solution with fixed $\xi$ and $\delta C_\xi=0$. Let $C_R$ be finite oriented smooth singular hypersurface chains with $\partial C_R=S_R-B$, where the boundary orientations are outward at $S_R$ and inward at $B$. Then
$$d(\delta Q_\xi-\iota_\xi\theta)=0$$
on each $C_R$, and
$$\delta H_\xi=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{S_R}(\delta Q_\xi-\iota_\xi\theta) =\int_B\delta Q_\xi =\frac{\hbar\kappa}{2\pi k_B}\,\delta S_W.$$
The last equality uses the derivative-free curvature hypothesis and the Noether entropy functional of the preceding theorem. The identity is conditional on the exact boundary-charge and vanishing-constraint assumptions; $\kappa$ is the unperturbed surface gravity. For the Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian $\mathcal L_{\rm EH}=R\boldsymbol\epsilon_g/(16\pi G)$ with Newton constant $G>0$ in the same $c=1$ action normalization, it gives $S_W=k_BA_B/(4G\hbar)$, where $A_B:=\int_B dA_B$.

statement.proposed:
Fix an upper endpoint $U_H\in\mathbb R$ and a scale $A>0$, both measured in seconds, and let $k>0$ be measured in seconds$^{-1}$. Let $u\in\mathbb R$ be the outgoing coordinate, measured in seconds, and define
$$U(u)=U_H-Ae^{-ku}.$$
Then $U$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R$ onto $(-\infty,U_H)$, with derivative $U'(u)=Ak e^{-ku}>0$; $U_H$ is only the upper-endpoint label in this channel. Let $\chi>0$ be a fixed conversion factor with units of length per second, and put $\ell(u)=\chi U(u)$ and $\ell_H=\chi U_H$. For $g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, let $u_\ell$ be the smooth inverse of $\ell$ and define $f_g(x)=g(u_\ell(x))$ for $x<\ell_H$, and $f_g(x)=0$ for $x\ge\ell_H$. The support of $g$ is compact, so $f_g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$. Define the channel current $j(g)=J(f_g)$ using the Fock-vacuum chiral current $J$, and set
$$W(g,h)=\langle\Omega,J(\overline{f_g})J(f_h)\Omega\rangle_2.$$
The associated two-point distribution is the diffeomorphism pullback of the supplied length-coordinate kernel $C_\ell(X-Y)=-\frac{1}{4\pi}(X-Y-i0)^{-2}$; in seconds coordinates its kernel is
$$K(u,v)=U'(u)U'(v)\left[-\frac{1}{4\pi}\bigl(U(u)-U(v)-i0\bigr)^{-2}\right].$$
Here $i0$ is the lower boundary obtained by testing the regularizations $-\frac{1}{4\pi}(s-i\epsilon)^{-2}$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$, and the pullback is defined by the smooth diffeomorphism, not by pointwise evaluation on the diagonal. The tested form is of positive type: $W(g,g)\ge0$ for every $g$.

For real-valued tests $g_1,\ldots,g_n$, write
$$M_n(g_1,\ldots,g_n)=\langle\Omega,J(f_{g_1})\cdots J(f_{g_n})\Omega\rangle_2.$$
This Fock-vacuum field is Gaussian in the precise sense that $M_n=0$ for odd $n$, while for even $n$ it is the sum over pair partitions $\pi$ of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ of $\prod_{(i,j)\in\pi,\ i<j}M_2(g_i,g_j)$, with each contraction ordered as displayed. This is an exact one-dimensional test-coordinate channel; it does not assert existence of four-dimensional collapse scattering.

statement.before:
Use the mathematical assumptions of the supplied chiral channel, including Countable Choice: every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. Adopt SI units. Let $c>0$ have units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $G>0$ have units $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\hbar>0$ have units $\mathrm{J\,s}$, and $k_B>0$ have units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mass $M>0$ is a fixed model parameter in kilograms. Use a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(\mathcal M,g)$ without boundary, of signature $(-+++)$. Global hyperbolicity means strong causality and compact causal diamonds $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$, where $J^\pm$ are defined by consistently directed causal curves; strong causality means every point has arbitrarily small neighborhoods that each causal curve meets in a connected parameter interval. A Hadamard bisolution is a distribution $W_2$ on $\mathcal M\times\mathcal M$ satisfying $P_xW_2=P_yW_2=0$ and $\operatorname{WF}(W_2)=\mathcal C_g^+$, the positive-frequency null relation whose pairs $(x,\xi;y,-\eta)$ have nonzero future-null covectors $\xi,\eta$ equal to a common positive multiple of the metric-dual tangent of one affinely parametrized future null geodesic at the two endpoints, with covector parallel transport and either endpoint parameter order; coincident endpoints have $\eta=\xi$. The manifold is the smooth domain on which this free-field model is posed; no singular interior is included.

Assume that after a smooth Cauchy surface $\Sigma_0$ (a spacelike hypersurface met exactly once by each inextendible causal curve of the modeled region), the modeled future exterior is exactly the Schwarzschild exterior of fixed mass $M$, with areal radius $r>r_s$, $r_s=2GM/c^2$, and metric
$$ds^2=-\left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right)c^2dt^2+\left(1-\frac{r_s}{r}\right)^{-1}dr^2+r^2(d\vartheta^2+\sin^2\vartheta\,d\varphi^2).$$
Here $t$ is the stationary Schwarzschild time in seconds, $r$ is in metres, and $\vartheta,\varphi$ are the usual dimensionless angular coordinates. The metric is a fixed background: the field does not change it. The retarded coordinate is $u=t-r_*/c$, where $r_*=r+r_s\log(r/r_s-1)$. The associated geometric surface-gravity parameter in inverse metres and its time-frequency version are, by this model's normalization,
$$\kappa_{\rm geom}:=\frac{1}{2r_s}=\frac{c^2}{4GM},\qquad k:=c\kappa_{\rm geom}=\frac{c^3}{4GM}>0.$$

Adopt one real, linear, massless, minimally coupled scalar field on $(\mathcal M,g)$. Its smooth classical solutions are $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathcal M;\mathbb R)$ satisfying $P\phi=0$ for $P:=-g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b$, where $\nabla$ is the unique torsion-free connection with $\nabla g=0$; the canonical scalar field has length degree $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$.

For its quantization, choose a complex Hilbert one-particle space $\mathcal H_{\rm in}$ with inner product conjugate-linear in the first variable and linear in the second; its dense incoming packet subspace is specified below. For $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal H_{\rm in,s}^{(n)}$ be the range of the symmetrizing projection $P_{s,n}:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ on the completed $n$-fold Hilbert tensor product, where $U_\pi$ permutes tensor factors, and put $\mathcal H_{\rm in,s}^{(0)}:=\mathbb C$. The bosonic Fock space is the Hilbert direct sum
$$\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_{\rm in}):=\left\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in\mathcal H_{\rm in,s}^{(n)},\ \sum_{n\ge0}\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with vacuum $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$ and finite-particle domain $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consisting of sequences with only finitely many nonzero components. On this domain, define creation and annihilation by $a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n:=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$ and $a_n(h)\Psi_n:=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$ for $n\ge1$, where $C_h(v):=\langle h,v\rangle$; set $a(h)\Omega=0$. The model supplies a continuous real-linear map $K:C_c^\infty(\mathcal M;\mathbb R)\to\mathcal H_{\rm in}$, for the standard test-function topology, the locally convex inductive-limit topology over compact supports of the fixed-support smooth-function spaces, whose seminorms are suprema of each finite order of coordinate derivatives on compact chart subsets, with $K(Pf)=0$, and defines the smeared field $\Phi(f):=a(Kf)+a^\dagger(Kf)$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real test functions the Fock commutation relations give $[\Phi(f),\Phi(g)]=2i\operatorname{Im}\langle Kf,Kg\rangle I$, where $I$ is the identity; thus $K$ fixes the commutator form of this adopted representation. Let $\mathfrak A$ be the unital complex $*$-algebra generated by all $a(h),a^\dagger(h)$ for $h\in\mathcal H_{\rm in}$, the smeared fields $\Phi(f)$, and the outgoing packet operators and their adjoints specified below. All generators and their adjoints preserve the common dense domain $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$; the involution is the Hilbert adjoint restricted to this domain, so every finite product used below belongs to $\mathfrak A$. Inclusion of the packet operators and existence of a state on this enlarged algebra satisfying all following conditions are adopted model premises, not consequences of the smearing map $K$. A state $\varpi$ is a positive normalized linear functional on that algebra, and its two-point distribution is $W_2(f,g)=\varpi(\Phi(f)\Phi(g))$. Require $W_2$ to be a Hadamard bisolution for $P$. The pairing uses $d{\rm vol}_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3|$. The one-particle space, map $K$, and state are adopted model data; their construction is not derived from collapse matter. Here positive normalized means complex-linear with $\varpi(T^*T)\ge0$ for every $T\in\mathfrak A$ and $\varpi(I)=1$.

Assume a smooth conformal completion $\overline{\mathcal M}$ with boundary defining function $\rho$ such that $\rho>0$ on $\mathcal M$, $\rho=0$ and $d\rho\ne0$ on the selected boundary components, and $\widetilde g=\rho^2g$ extends smoothly as a nondegenerate Lorentzian metric with those components null hypersurfaces. Denote the past and future null components by $\mathscr I^-$ and $\mathscr I^+$; they are the asymptotic endpoints of incoming and outgoing null rays in this model. Fix a smooth affine parameter $v$ in seconds on the generators of $\mathscr I^-$, relative to $\widetilde g$ (so $\widetilde\nabla_{\partial_v}\partial_v=0$). The dense incoming positive-frequency one-particle packet subspace consists of the model's incoming mode packets with Fourier dependence $e^{-i\omega v}$, where $\omega>0$ is angular frequency in radians per second and radians are dimensionless. For every packet $h$ in this subspace, write $a_{\rm in}(h):=a(h)$; the incoming ground-state condition means $\varpi(a_{\rm in}(h)^*a_{\rm in}(h))=0$. This free-field equation, quantization, state, and asymptotic structure are adopted, not derived assumptions.

For each outgoing retarded-time coordinate $u$, measured in seconds, adopt the increasing null-ray label
$$U(u)=U_H-Ae^{-ku},\qquad U_H\in\mathbb R\ {\rm seconds},\quad A>0\ {\rm seconds}.$$
The two-point current channel for this label is exactly the tested exponential channel defined by the ray map above. It is the time-coordinate version of the reduced exponential-current branch, whose length flow parameter is $u_{\rm geom}=cu$, inverse-length parameter is $\kappa_{\rm geom}=k/c$, and detailed-balance convention is the same. The identification of the four-dimensional near-horizon packet channel with this one-dimensional tested current is an adopted model premise, not a restriction theorem for a four-dimensional field. The separate accelerated-detector and two-state-rate branch is not part of this collapse model.

Let $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$ label the degree of a spherical-harmonic angular channel; no sum over its magnetic degeneracy is taken. For angular frequency $\omega>0$, measured in radians per second (radians are dimensionless), let $\Gamma_\ell(\omega)\in[0,1]$ be the dimensionless transmission probability supplied by the stationary radial-scattering model. Assume $\Gamma_\ell$ is continuous on every compact frequency interval $K=[\omega_-,\omega_+]\subset(0,\infty)$ with $\omega_-<\omega_+$. By definition in this model, the normalized near-horizon signal mode $a_{\ell,\omega}$ and independent incoming vacuum mode $e_{\ell,\omega}$ are mapped to the outgoing mode $b_{\ell,\omega}$ and its complementary mode $d_{\ell,\omega}$ by
$$\begin{pmatrix}b_{\ell,\omega}\\d_{\ell,\omega}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{\Gamma_\ell(\omega)}&\sqrt{1-\Gamma_\ell(\omega)}\\-\sqrt{1-\Gamma_\ell(\omega)}&\sqrt{\Gamma_\ell(\omega)}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a_{\ell,\omega}\\e_{\ell,\omega}\end{pmatrix}.$$
All four mode operators use the unit one-particle normalization of the supplied channel, so their occupations are dimensionless. The squared coefficient $\Gamma_\ell(\omega)$ is the transmitted fraction; no transmission coefficient is calculated here.

In the adopted frequency-diagonal Fock interpretation, the positive-frequency Fourier coefficient of the ordered current two-point function is $\omega/2$ times the mode occupation. Thus the occupation associated with spectral coefficient $S_k(\omega)$ is, by this model's normalization, $2S_k(\omega)/\omega$ for $\omega>0$. This identification is part of the adopted channel model; it is not a detector response or an observed particle count.

For each compact frequency interval $K=[\omega_-,\omega_+]\subset(0,\infty)$ with $\omega_-<\omega_+$, the packet Hilbert space is $\mathcal H_K=L^2(K,d\omega)$ with $\langle f,g\rangle_K:=\int_K\overline{f(\omega)}g(\omega)d\omega$. Write $C_c^\infty(K;\mathbb C)$ for zero extensions to $K$ of smooth functions compactly supported in $(\omega_-,\omega_+)$. A normalized packet is an $f\in C_c^\infty(K;\mathbb C)$ with $\int_K|f(\omega)|^2d\omega=1$; $f$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{1/2}$. For each $s\in\mathbb R$, the model supplies a bounded sesquilinear form $B_{\ell,s}:\mathcal H_K\times\mathcal H_K\to\mathbb C$, conjugate-linear in its first entry and linear in its second. The model supplies conjugate-linear packet maps $f\mapsto a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(f)$ on $\mathcal H_K$ with operators and adjoints preserving $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, satisfying $[a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(f),a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(g)^*]=\langle f,g\rangle_K I$ and $[a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(f),a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(g)]=0$ there. On smooth packets its value is
$$B_{\ell,s}(f,g):=\varpi\!\left(a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(g)^*a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(f)\right),$$
where $a_{\ell,\mathrm{out},s}(f)$ is the annihilation operator of the packet translated to retarded-time center $s$ seconds at $\mathscr I^+$. The reversed order of the labels $g,f$ makes $B_{\ell,s}$ conjugate-linear in $f$ and linear in $g$ with the stated annihilator convention; its diagonal remains the number expectation. Boundedness on $\mathcal H_K$ is an assumed moment bound, not boundedness of the operators themselves.

state restricted to one side of the deformed cut, equivalently to the
corresponding side of a Cauchy surface; the entropy itself may be divergent,
while the source-defined derivatives in the inequality are finite. With a
regulator admitting a positive trace-one reduced density operator $\rho$, the
von Neumann entropy is $-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$, with
$0\log0=0$; continuum entropy and its derivatives use the cited limiting
prescription, not an assumed finite unregulated density matrix. In §2,
equation (2.2), the authors call the pointwise formulation the “general
conjecture”; its local geometric condition is that the classical expansion
and shear vanish at $p$. For $d>2$ and a transverse patch of area $A$ about $p$,
$S_{\mathrm{out}}''(p)$ is the source-defined second affine variation for
that patch, with the other generators held fixed. The corresponding
pointwise formulation, in the small-area notation of equation (2.3), is
$$\langle T_{kk}(p)\rangle\ge\frac{1}{2\pi}\lim_{A\to0}\frac{S_{\mathrm{out}}''(p)}{A},\qquad \langle T_{kk}(p)\rangle:=\langle T_{ab}(p)k^ak^b\rangle.$$
Here $A$ is the geometric area of the transverse patch, computed from the
Riemannian metric induced on $\Sigma$, so $[A]=L^{d-2}$; both sides then have
dimension $L^{-d}$. Separately, the paper's abstract and
outline state applicability to free or superrenormalizable, massive or massless
bosonic fields on stationary null hypersurfaces, where “stationary” means that
the classical expansion vanishes everywhere. The authors explicitly treat the
QNEC proof as a fixed-background calculation without dynamical gravity. Its
§3.1–§4.5 argument treats $D>2$ on such a hypersurface. Section 5 derives the
free-scalar $D=2$ inequality
$\langle T_{2D}\rangle\ge(2\pi)^{-1}S''_{2D}$ by dimensional reduction
and strong subadditivity, with no shrinking transverse-area limit;
there $T_{2D}$ is the stress tensor of the reduced chiral scalar, whose action
on the reduced theory agrees with the transverse integral of $T_{kk}$, and
$S''_{2D}$ is the reduced entropy's second affine variation. Section 5 also
treats higher-spin bosonic fields and discusses extending the result to
superrenormalizable interactions conditionally on preservation of the
null-surface observable algebra and $T_{kk}$; the paper presents that
preservation as expected, not as established for arbitrary such interactions.
These source-reported scopes are distinct from the general pointwise
conjectural formulation of §2; they do not establish that formulation for every
field theory and background.

For the quantum focusing conjecture (QFC) in the cited semiclassical
Einstein-gravity formulation, use the geometry above and let $\sigma$ be a
smooth spacelike
codimension-two cut splitting a Cauchy surface, and let $\mathcal N$ be the
smooth null hypersurface generated by its orthogonal future-directed null
geodesics. Label the generators by local transverse coordinates
$y=(y^1,\ldots,y^{d-2})$ in $d$ spacetime dimensions. On each generator choose
an affine parameter $\lambda$ increasing to the future, with $\lambda=0$ at
$\sigma$, $[\lambda]=L$, and tangent $k=(d/d\lambda)$. A smooth
nonnegative function
$V(y)$ defines a cut $\sigma[V]$ by its intersection with generator $y$ at
$\lambda=V(y)$; restrict to profiles for which this is a well-defined smooth
cut that still splits a Cauchy surface. Let $q_{AB}[V]$ be the positive
induced metric on $\sigma[V]$ in the coordinates $y$, set
$h[V](y):=\det(q_{AB}[V](y))$, and define its area by
$$A[V]:=\int_{\sigma[V]}\sqrt{h[V](y)}\,d^{d-2}y.$$
For $d=2$, a cut is discrete, the empty metric determinant is $1$, and
this integral is counting measure; functional derivatives are derivatives
with respect to the individual cut-point displacements. The JT formulation
below uses a different gravitational entropy term and normalization.
Let $S_{\mathrm{out}}[V]$ be the von Neumann entropy of the quantum-field state
restricted to one side of $\sigma[V]$. It may be ultraviolet divergent by
itself. The cited source defines the generalized entropy by the following
combination and assumes its renormalized value is finite and cutoff-independent:
$$S_{\mathrm{gen}}[V]:=\frac{A[V]}{4G}+S_{\mathrm{out}}[V]+S_{\mathrm{ct}}[V],$$
where $S_{\mathrm{ct}}[V]$ is the source-prescribed local geometric
counterterm contribution; this is the source's $S_{\mathrm{grav}}[V]
=A[V]/(4G)+S_{\mathrm{ct}}[V]$ plus $S_{\mathrm{out}}[V]$, with
$\hbar=1$. In $d$ dimensions, $G>0$ has dimension $L^{d-2}$, so
$S_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is dimensionless. The source defines the quantum expansion
as the entropy response to a localized affine displacement, divided by the
geometric area of the transverse patch; in its functional-derivative
convention this is
$$\Theta[V;y_1]:=\frac{4G}{\sqrt{h[V](y_1)}}\frac{\delta S_{\mathrm{gen}}[V]}{\delta V(y_1)}.$$
For every admissible one-parameter family $V_\tau$ with
$\partial_\tau V_\tau(y)\ge0$, the QFC conjectures
$$\frac{\delta\Theta[V;y_1]}{\delta V(y_2)}\le0$$
for all generator labels $y_1,y_2$, with the coincident-point diagonal
understood in the source's distributional sense. This remains a conjecture in
general.

The cited 2017 Einstein-Hilbert-Gauss-Bonnet analysis constructs weak-curvature
QFC violations for $d\ge5$ at points where the null expansion and shear vanish.
The construction uses arbitrarily fine transverse localization. The authors'
v2 note reports that restricting entropy variations to surfaces smooth on the
scale associated with $G\gamma$ removes their violation, and leaves the
effective-field-theory-scale formulation as an open issue.

The cited 2026 v3 paper proves the restricted QFC (rQFC) for a class of
two-dimensional Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity models coupled to quantum field
theory, in regions where the total dilaton is positive and the matter state
satisfies the source's two-dimensional QNEC. The total dilaton is the smooth
scalar $\Phi=\phi_0+\phi:M\to\mathbb R$ of that two-dimensional model,
with constant $\phi_0$; it replaces transverse area in the entropy term.
For a moving cut point $P(\lambda)$ on a future affine null geodesic,
$\lambda\in I\subset\mathbb R$, keep the other cut points fixed and use
$S_{\mathrm{gen}}=\sum_i\Phi(P_i)/(4G)+S_{\mathrm{ren}}$, where
$S_{\mathrm{ren}}$ is the source-renormalized matter entropy. Here $G>0$
and $\Phi$ are dimensionless, and the source's quantum expansion is
$\Theta(\lambda)=4G\Phi(P(\lambda))^{-1}dS_{\mathrm{gen}}/d\lambda$,
with $\Phi(P(\lambda))>0$ and the derivatives assumed to exist. Its rQFC
asserts $d\Theta/d\lambda\le0$ where $\Theta=0$; this is weaker than
requiring that inequality at every cut. The authors also construct
full-QFC counterexamples in a JT regime where matter quantum effects compete
with the total dilaton. They state that this regime has no higher-dimensional
uplift; although the JT action has an approximate dimensional-reduction origin,
they treat this counterexample regime as an exact two-dimensional toy model
and caution that it is not strong evidence against the original QFC. These
theory- and regime-specific findings establish no universal QFC theorem for
arbitrary higher-curvature effective gravity. The linearized horizon model
discussed here defines no outside entropy, generalized-entropy functional, or
entropy shape derivative; it neither assumes nor derives QNEC or QFC.
statement.proposed:
The QNEC and QFC claims above are reported source formulations, not local
proof premises. The higher-curvature result is limited to the models and
dimensions in its cited analysis; its discussion also distinguishes the
pointwise conjecture from possible effective-field-theory resolution
conditions.

statement.proposed:
Let $I$ be a finite nonempty index set. For each $\alpha\in I$, let $H_\alpha$ and $K_\alpha$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, and give

$$H_A:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}(H_\alpha\otimes K_\alpha)$$

the orthogonal direct-sum inner product: distinct summands are orthogonal and the inner product within a summand is the Hilbert tensor-product inner product. On elementary tensors that inner product is $\langle x\otimes y,x'\otimes y'\rangle=\langle x,x'\rangle\langle y,y'\rangle$. A map $T\otimes U$ acts by $(T\otimes U)(x\otimes y)=Tx\otimes Uy$, and a direct-sum map acts blockwise with zero off-diagonal blocks.

A complex-linear endomorphism is a linear map from a vector space to itself. A density matrix on a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space is a self-adjoint endomorphism with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one; it is faithful when all eigenvalues are strictly positive. These are the conventions used for the finite density matrices in the earlier modular-balance result. The summand indexed by $\alpha$ is called the $\alpha$ sector. For each $\alpha$, fix a faithful density matrix $\chi_\alpha$ on $K_\alpha$. Let $\mathbf p=(p_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}$ satisfy $p_\alpha>0$ and $\sum_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha=1$, and let $\rho_\alpha$ be density matrices on $H_\alpha$. Define the encoded endomorphism

$$\mathcal E_\chi(\mathbf p,\rho):=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha\,\rho_\alpha\otimes\chi_\alpha.$$

When this encoded endomorphism is a density matrix, call it the encoded reduced state. The logical data are $\mathbf p$ and $\{\rho_\alpha\}$; the ancillary matrices $\{\chi_\alpha\}$ are held fixed. For a second strictly positive probability vector $\mathbf q$ and faithful density matrices $\sigma_\alpha$ on the same $H_\alpha$, write $\sigma_A:=\mathcal E_\chi(\mathbf q,\sigma)$ for the encoded reference endomorphism.

This is a finite-dimensional algebraic model. The definition makes no gravitational interpretation and does not identify a matrix entropy term with a geometric area.

statement.proposed:
Let $I$ be a finite nonempty set. For each $\alpha\in I$, let $H_\alpha,K_\alpha$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces. A density matrix is a self-adjoint endomorphism with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one; it is faithful when all its eigenvalues are strictly positive. Let $p_\alpha,q_\alpha>0$ with $\sum_\alpha p_\alpha=\sum_\alpha q_\alpha=1$, let $\rho_\alpha$ be a density matrix on $H_\alpha$, let $\sigma_\alpha$ be a faithful density matrix on $H_\alpha$, and let $\chi_\alpha$ be a fixed faithful density matrix on $K_\alpha$. Form the finite orthogonal direct sums

$$\rho_A:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha\rho_\alpha\otimes\chi_\alpha,\qquad \sigma_A:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}q_\alpha\sigma_\alpha\otimes\chi_\alpha.$$

For a density matrix $\tau$, set $s(\tau):=-\sum_{\lambda_j(\tau)>0}\lambda_j(\tau)\log\lambda_j(\tau)$, with $0\log0:=0$, so entropy is in nats. For density matrices $\tau,\omega$ with faithful reference $\omega$, set $D(\tau\|\omega):=\operatorname{tr}(\tau\log\tau)-\operatorname{tr}(\tau\log\omega)$ using spectral logarithms on positive eigenvalues. Also define $H(\mathbf p):=-\sum_\alpha p_\alpha\log p_\alpha$ and $D_{\rm cl}(\mathbf p\|\mathbf q):=\sum_\alpha p_\alpha\log(p_\alpha/q_\alpha)$. Then $\rho_A$ and $\sigma_A$ are density matrices, $\sigma_A$ is faithful, and

$$s(\rho_A)=H(\mathbf p)+\sum_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha\bigl(s(\rho_\alpha)+s(\chi_\alpha)\bigr),$$

$$D(\rho_A\|\sigma_A)=D_{\rm cl}(\mathbf p\|\mathbf q)+\sum_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha D(\rho_\alpha\|\sigma_\alpha).$$

These are exact finite-dimensional matrix identities; no literal black-hole area, universal Ryu–Takayanagi formula, continuum limit, or gravitational entropy claim follows.

statement.proposed:
Take two sectors with probabilities $p_1,p_2>0$ and $p_1+p_2=1$. Let $H_1,H_2$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, choose density matrices $\rho_1,\rho_2$ on them, and choose $q_1,q_2>0$ with $q_1+q_2=1$ and faithful reference density matrices $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ on the same spaces. Let the first ancillary space be one-dimensional with $\chi_1=[1]$, and let the second be $\mathbb C^d$ for an integer $d\ge1$, with $\chi_2=I_d/d$. The encoded state has entropy

$$s(\rho_A)=H(p_1,p_2)+p_1s(\rho_1)+p_2s(\rho_2)+p_2\log d,$$

where $H(p_1,p_2):=-p_1\log p_1-p_2\log p_2$ is the sector-probability entropy in nats. The sector-probability contribution is $H(p_1,p_2)$ and the ancillary contribution is $p_2\log d$; when $d=1$, the ancillary contribution is zero. This is an exact finite matrix example and asserts no literal black-hole area law.

statement.before:
Fix a named, positively oriented SI laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$ and angular frequency $\omega>0$. Adopt the SI constants and
coordinate units of the laboratory convention: $c>0$ is in m s$^{-1}$,
$k_0:=\omega/c$ is in m$^{-1}$, and electric-field components are in V
m$^{-1}$. Let
$\Pi=\{(x,y,z_0):(x,y)\in D\}$ be a specified reference plane, where
$z_0\in\mathbb R$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a specified nonempty region.
Its oriented orthonormal transverse basis is $(e_x,e_y)$ and its normal is
$e_z$.

For the paraxial context, adopt $c>0$, $k_0=\omega/c$, and
$0<\delta<1$. The angular-spectrum variable $\xi\in\mathbb R^2$ is measured
in cycles per metre, $q=2\pi\xi$ is in m$^{-1}$, and the forward propagating
cone is $D_\delta=\{\xi:|q|\le\delta k_0\}$ with
$k_z(\xi)=\sqrt{k_0^2-|q|^2}>0$. The matrix below is defined pointwise for the
two-component projection; it does not assert that an arbitrary random
superposition is an exact Maxwell field or that the individual-mode
longitudinal bound extends to an ensemble without additional hypotheses.

Let $(\Xi,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a specified probability space. At each
fixed $\rho\in D$, let $Z_\rho:\Xi\to\mathbb C^2$ be measurable, with four real
coordinates
$X_\rho=(\operatorname{Re}Z_x,\operatorname{Im}Z_x,
\operatorname{Re}Z_y,\operatorname{Im}Z_y)$ forming a square-integrable
$\mathbb R^4$ random vector and
$\mathbb E[|Z_x(\rho)|^2+|Z_y(\rho)|^2]<\infty$. For $\sigma\in\Xi$, the
associated transverse real-field model is
$E_\perp(\rho,\sigma,t)=\operatorname{Re}(Z_\rho(\sigma)e^{-i\omega t})$.
Expectation is taken over this declared classical ensemble and is applied
componentwise to complex integrable variables. Define
$$\Gamma(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_\rho Z_\rho^\dagger],\qquad \Gamma_{ij}(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_i(\rho)\overline{Z_j(\rho)}]\quad(i,j\in\{1,2\}).$$
Thus $\Gamma$ is the uncentered second-moment matrix of the two selected
components; no zero-mean assumption is made. The degree of polarization is
defined only when $S_0>0$ by
$$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22},\quad S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22},\quad S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12},\quad S_3:=-2\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{12},\qquad \mathcal P:=\frac{\sqrt{S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2}}{S_0}.$$
The minus sign in $S_3$ is fixed by the stated phasor convention and the
ordered basis $(e_x,e_y)$. In this two-component model, a positive-intensity
state is called unpolarized when $\Gamma=(S_0/2)I_2$; this label concerns
second moments and does not say that any realization is a quantum state.
The $S_j$ have units (V m$^{-1}$)$^2$; $S_0$ is a mean-square field coordinate,
not an absolutely calibrated irradiance.

The construction applies to any ordered pair of square-integrable classical
complex amplitudes. When the pair labels transverse electric components,
$S_j$ have the polarization interpretation just defined. When it labels two
beam channels, the same matrix entries are channel correlations; they are not
polarization components.
statement.proposed:
Fix a named, positively oriented SI laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$ and angular frequency $\omega>0$. Adopt the SI constants and
coordinate units of the laboratory convention: $c>0$ is in m s$^{-1}$,
$k_0:=\omega/c$ is in m$^{-1}$, and electric-field components are in V
m$^{-1}$. Let
$\Pi=\{(x,y,z_0):(x,y)\in D\}$ be a specified reference plane, where
$z_0\in\mathbb R$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a specified nonempty region.
Let $(e_x,e_y,e_z)$ be the positively oriented orthonormal coordinate basis of
the chart. The ordered transverse basis of $\Pi$ is $(e_x,e_y)$ and its normal
is $e_z$.

For the paraxial context, adopt $c>0$, $k_0=\omega/c$, and
$0<\delta<1$. The angular-spectrum variable $\xi\in\mathbb R^2$ is measured
in cycles per metre, $q=2\pi\xi$ is in m$^{-1}$, and the forward propagating
cone is $D_\delta=\{\xi:|q|\le\delta k_0\}$ with
$k_z(\xi)=\sqrt{k_0^2-|q|^2}>0$. Here $|q|:=\sqrt{q_x^2+q_y^2}$. The matrix
below is defined pointwise for the
two-component projection; it does not assert that an arbitrary random
superposition is an exact Maxwell field or that the individual-mode
longitudinal bound extends to an ensemble without additional hypotheses.

Let $(\Xi,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a specified probability space. Identify
$\mathbb C^2$ with $\mathbb R^4$ by real and imaginary coordinates and equip it
with the Euclidean Borel $\sigma$-algebra; measurable maps to $\mathbb C^2$
are understood with respect to this $\sigma$-algebra. At each fixed
$\rho\in D$, let $Z_\rho:\Xi\to\mathbb C^2$ be measurable. Let
$\pi_x,\pi_y:\mathbb C^2\to\mathbb C$ be the first and second continuous
coordinate projections, and define the coordinate random variables
$Z_x(\rho):=\pi_x\circ Z_\rho:\Xi\to\mathbb C$ and
$Z_y(\rho):=\pi_y\circ Z_\rho:\Xi\to\mathbb C$. Thus
$Z_\rho(\sigma)=(Z_x(\rho)(\sigma),Z_y(\rho)(\sigma))^{\mathsf T}$ for
$\sigma\in\Xi$. The map $X_\rho:\Xi\to\mathbb R^4$ is defined by the four
real coordinate maps of $Z_\rho$; these maps are continuous, so $X_\rho$ is
measurable as their composition with $Z_\rho$.
No joint measurability in $\rho$ is assumed or used. Define
$$X_\rho(\sigma):=(\operatorname{Re}Z_x(\rho)(\sigma),\operatorname{Im}Z_x(\rho)(\sigma),\operatorname{Re}Z_y(\rho)(\sigma),\operatorname{Im}Z_y(\rho)(\sigma)).$$
Since
$|X_\rho(\sigma)|^2=|Z_x(\rho)(\sigma)|^2+|Z_y(\rho)(\sigma)|^2$,
assume $X_\rho$ is square-integrable, equivalently
$\mathbb E[|Z_x(\rho)|^2+|Z_y(\rho)|^2]<\infty$. For $\rho\in D$,
$\sigma\in\Xi$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, define the associated transverse
real-field model by
$E_\perp(\rho,\sigma,t):=\operatorname{Re}(Z_\rho(\sigma)e^{-i\omega t})$,
where $\operatorname{Re}$ is applied componentwise. Expectation is taken over
this declared classical ensemble and is applied componentwise to complex
integrable variables. Regard vectors in $\mathbb C^2$ as columns. For a column
$w=(w_1,w_2)^{\mathsf T}$ define $w^\dagger:=(\overline{w_1},\overline{w_2})$;
for a $2\times2$ matrix $M$ define $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$,
where $\overline M$ is obtained by conjugating each entry. Put
$Z_1(\rho):=Z_x(\rho)$ and $Z_2(\rho):=Z_y(\rho)$. Define
$$\Gamma(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_\rho Z_\rho^\dagger],\qquad \Gamma_{ij}(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_i(\rho)\overline{Z_j(\rho)}]\quad(i,j\in\{1,2\}).$$
Thus $\Gamma$ is the uncentered second-moment matrix of the two selected
components; no zero-mean assumption is made. At each fixed $\rho$, suppressing
the argument $\rho$ in these coordinate names, define the Stokes coordinates
$$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22},\quad S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22},\quad S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12},\quad S_3:=-2\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{12}.$$
When $S_0>0$, define the degree of polarization by
$$\mathcal P:=\frac{\sqrt{S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2}}{S_0}.$$
The minus sign in $S_3$ is fixed by the stated phasor convention and the
ordered basis $(e_x,e_y)$. In this two-component model, call the ensemble at
$\rho$ unpolarized when $S_0>0$ and $\Gamma=(S_0/2)I_2$, where $I_2$ is the
$2\times2$ identity matrix; this label concerns second moments and does not
say that any realization is a quantum state.
For the transverse electric-field interpretation, the $S_j$ have units
(V m$^{-1}$)$^2$; $S_0$ is a mean-square field coordinate, not an absolutely
calibrated irradiance.

The same algebraic construction applies to any ordered pair of square-integrable
classical complex amplitudes of a common physical unit; the second moments then
have the square of that unit. When the pair labels transverse electric
components, the $S_j$ have the polarization interpretation just defined. When
it labels two beam channels, the same matrix entries are channel correlations;
they are not polarization components.

statement.proposed:
Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty oriented smooth three-manifold without boundary. Let $\bar h$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $\psi\in C^\infty(\Sigma,(0,\infty))$, let $\bar E,\bar B$ be smooth contravariant vector fields, let $\bar A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor with $\bar h^{ij}\bar A_{ij}=0$, let $\tau\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\mathbb R)$, and let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be constant. Let $c,G,\mu_0>0$ and $\kappa=8\pi G/c^4$ be the parameters of the inherited SI-to-geometric dictionary, and set $\alpha=\sqrt{\kappa/(2\mu_0)}>0$. Define

$$h:=\psi^4\bar h,\qquad K:=\frac{\tau}{3}h+\psi^{-2}\bar A,\qquad E:=\psi^{-6}\bar E,\qquad B:=\psi^{-6}\bar B.$$

The fields $E$ and $B$ are geometric-normalized spatial vectors: in length coordinates their components have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Their SI-convention counterparts are $e:=\alpha^{-1}E$ and $b:=\alpha^{-1}B$. This definition imposes no divergence, Hamiltonian, or momentum equation and asserts no existence, uniqueness, or spacetime development.

statement.proposed:
Use the smooth conformal seed data defined in this development on an oriented smooth three-manifold, and let $D$ and $\bar D$ be the Levi-Civita connections of $h=\psi^4\bar h$ and $\bar h$. Define $\Delta_{\bar h}\psi:=\bar h^{ij}\bar D_i\partial_j\psi$, with the Euclidean convention $\Delta=\sum_i\partial_i^2$ in Cartesian coordinates. Use the spatial curvature sign and scalar-curvature contraction fixed for induced data in the preceding Gauss-Codazzi convention. Let $e=\alpha^{-1}\psi^{-6}\bar E$ and $b=\alpha^{-1}\psi^{-6}\bar B$ be the SI-convention vector fields associated with the inherited constrained electrovacuum initial-data convention. Then the two Maxwell divergence constraints are equivalent to

$$\bar D_i\bar E^i=0,\qquad \bar D_i\bar B^i=0,$$

and the SI Hamiltonian constraint in that definition is equivalent to

$$-8\Delta_{\bar h}\psi+\bar R\,\psi-|\bar A|_{\bar h}^2\psi^{-7}+\left(\frac{2}{3}\tau^2-2\Lambda\right)\psi^5-2\left(|\bar E|_{\bar h}^2+|\bar B|_{\bar h}^2\right)\psi^{-3}=0.$$

Here $\bar R$ is the scalar curvature of $\bar h$ in the stated convention, and the barred norms use $\bar h$ to raise and lower indices. The exact vector divergence identities are $D_iE^i=\psi^{-6}\bar D_i\bar E^i$ and $D_iB^i=\psi^{-6}\bar D_i\bar B^i$. The separate momentum constraint remains

$$D^jK_{ji}-D_i\tau=-2\psi^{-6}(\bar E\times_{\bar h}\bar B)_i,$$

where the cross product on the right is lowered with $\bar h$. In particular, if $K=0$ and $\bar E\times_{\bar h}\bar B=0$, the momentum equation holds. The transformed scalar equation alone does not impose the momentum constraint and gives no elliptic existence theorem.

statement.proposed:
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be an oriented, time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, with metric-selected Levi-Civita connection $\nabla$. Let $\mathcal U\subseteq M$ be open, let $u,V,s\in C^\infty(\mathcal U,\mathbb R)$, and let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $\mathcal U$. Define
$$\Box_g u:=\nabla^a\nabla_a u,\qquad |du|_g^2:=g^{ab}(\nabla_a u)(\nabla_b u).$$
If $\Box_g u=Vu+s$, define the symmetric covariant tensor
$$T_{ab}[u,V]:=(\nabla_a u)(\nabla_b u)-\frac12g_{ab}\bigl(|du|_g^2+Vu^2\bigr),$$
the vector current $J_X^a:=g^{ac}T_{cb}X^b$, and the scalar deformation term $K_X:=T_{ab}\nabla^{(a}X^{b)}$, where $\nabla^{(a}X^{b)}=(\nabla^aX^b+\nabla^bX^a)/2$.

For a finite smooth singular $3$-chain $\Sigma=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\sigma_i$ with $k\ge0$ and $c_i\in\mathbb R$, take each simplex $\sigma_i$ to be a map $\Delta^3\to\mathcal U$ that extends smoothly to a map into $M$ on an open neighborhood of $\Delta^3$ in its affine span. Here
$$\Delta^3:=\{(t_0,t_1,t_2,t_3)\in\mathbb R^4:t_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j=0}^3t_j=1\},$$
with its standard orientation from the ordered vertices $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$, where each $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^4$. Define the local flux by
$$\Phi_{J_X}(\Sigma):=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i\int_{\Delta^3}\sigma_i^*(\iota_{J_X}\mathrm{vol}_g).$$

Here $\mathrm{vol}_g$ is the oriented metric $4$-form whose expression in an oriented chart is $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and $\iota_{J_X}\mathrm{vol}_g$ is the $3$-form that sends $(Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)\in(T_pM)^3$ to $\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(J_X(p),Y_1,Y_2,Y_3)$ at each $p\in\mathcal U$. The map $\sigma_i^*$ is pullback of differential forms, and each simplex integral uses the pullback form-integration convention of the metric-volume current-flux definition listed in the following references section. Linearity makes the sum independent of the written chain representation. The integral uses the differential-form convention on null faces and assigns no flux to a chain with points outside $\mathcal U$; it never extends $J_X$ outside $\mathcal U$. In length coordinates, if $u$ has unit $[u]$, then $V$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$, $s$ has unit $[u]\mathrm m^{-2}$, and the components of $T$ have unit $[u]^2\mathrm m^{-2}$; no physical normalization of $u$ or $X$ is imposed.

Use the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^N$. For $v:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^N$, define $\|v\|_2^2:=\int_{\mathbb R}|v|^2\,dx$ and $\|v\|_{H^1}^2:=\int_{\mathbb R}(|v|^2+|v_x|^2)\,dx$.

For every integer $N\ge1$, every smooth real symmetric $N\times N$ matrix potential $V(x)$ on $\mathbb R$, and every smooth solution $U:\mathbb R_t\times\mathbb R_x\to\mathbb R^N$ such that, for every nonempty compact $K\subset\mathbb R$, integer $k\ge0$, and integer $m\ge0$,
$$\sup_{t\in K,\ x\in\mathbb R}(1+|x|)^m|\partial_x^kU(t,x)|<\infty,$$
the solution of
$$U_{tt}-U_{xx}+V(x)U=0$$
has a finite constant $C(V,N)$, depending only on $V$ and $N$, such that
$$\|U(t,\cdot)\|_{H^1(\mathbb R)}+\|U_t(t,\cdot)\|_2\le C(V,N)\bigl(\|U(0,\cdot)\|_{H^1(\mathbb R)}+\|U_t(0,\cdot)\|_2\bigr)\quad(t\ge0).$$

statement.proposed:
Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|<M$. Put
$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad r>r_+.$$
Use the static exterior
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$
with the electric specialization $q_e=Q$, $q_m=0$, and $t=x^0$ of the
Reissner--Nordström metric and potential fixed in the preceding definition.
Thus
$$g=-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad A_t\longrightarrow0\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty).$$
Here $r_+$ is the positive outer root in the selected local model, not a claim
about an event horizon in a maximal spacetime. Set
$$\Phi_H:=\lim_{r\to\infty}A_t(r)-\lim_{r\downarrow r_+}A_t(r)=\frac{Q}{r_+}.$$
These are endpoint limits: $r=r_+$ and $r=\infty$ are not points of
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}$.

For $e\in\mathbb R$, use the trivial complex line bundle
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}\times\mathbb C$ and regard $\psi$ as a smooth map
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}\to\mathbb C$. In a product chart put
$D_a\psi:=(\partial_a-ieA_a)\psi$. Define the massless
charged wave operator in the static chart by
$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi,\qquad D_t=\partial_t+\frac{ieQ}{r}.$$
The equation used here is $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$; it is a fixed-background,
minimally coupled test-field equation and does not evolve or source $g$ or $A$.

Let $\omega>0$ and $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$. Supply a smooth
real function $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y.$$
No existence assertion about $Y$ is made. Use the tortoise coordinate
$$r_*(r):=\int_{2r_+}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho,$$
which is strictly increasing because $f>0$ on the exterior. Under the
subextremal hypotheses the supplied RN scalar-coordinate result proves that
$r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$; hence
$r_*\to-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$ and $r_*\to+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$.
A separated mode has the form
$$\psi(t,r,\Omega)=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)\frac{u(r_*)}{r},$$
where $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$ is a fixed incident amplitude with units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m$, $u\in C^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ is the normalized
radial function, and its reflection and transmission coefficients are
dimensionless.

Write $\omega_H:=\omega-e\Phi_H=\omega-eQ/r_+$ and, for any reference length
$L>0$, define the Coulomb phase
$$\Theta(r_*):=\omega r_*-eQ\log(r/L),\qquad \Theta'(r_*):=\omega-\frac{eQf(r)}r.$$
A normalized scattering solution is a smooth radial solution of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ for which, for some $R,T\in\mathbb C$,
$$u=e^{-i\Theta}+R e^{i\Theta}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\Theta'e^{-i\Theta}+i\Theta'R e^{i\Theta}+o(1)\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and
$$u=T e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\omega_HTe^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1)\quad(r\downarrow r_+).$$
The error terms tend to zero in the indicated limits. These boundary
conditions prescribe unit incoming amplitude at infinity. When $\omega_H\ne0$,
the condition as $r_*\to-\infty$ selects the $e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}$ branch at
the outer-root end. At $\omega_H=0$, the two exponential phases coincide, so
the condition does not distinguish ingoing from outgoing directions. They
define admissible scattering data; they assert neither existence nor
uniqueness of such a solution.

The logarithm in $\Theta$ is required by the long-range term
$-2\omega eQ/r$ in the asymptotic radial coefficient. Changing $L$ changes
constant phases, not flux magnitudes. All scattering data here use the gauge
$A_t(\infty)=0$, so the mode label $\omega$ is the asymptotic
gauge-covariant frequency. Under a constant shift $A_t'=A_t+C$, the field
transformation $\psi'=e^{ieCt}\psi$ changes the coordinate mode label to
$\omega'=\omega-eC$. The asymptotic kinetic frequency
$$\omega_\infty:=\omega+e\lim_{r\to\infty}A_t(r)$$
is invariant because
$$\omega'+e\lim_{r\to\infty}A_t'=\omega_\infty,$$
and $\Phi_H$ is invariant because the constant cancels from its difference.
Thus the invariant horizon frequency is $\omega_\infty-e\Phi_H$, which equals
$\omega_H=\omega-e\Phi_H$ in the chosen gauge.

Use geometric units $G=c=1$ and length coordinates, with
$[t]=[r]=[r_*]=[M]=[Q]=[L]=\mathrm m$,
$[e]=[\omega]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, $f$ dimensionless, and $A_t$ dimensionless;
then $\Theta$ is dimensionless and each term in $\Box_{g,A}$ has units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The coupling $e$ is the charge coupling in the
chosen field normalization. This item uses geometric units and asserts no SI
value or conversion for $e$.
This definition excludes scalar mass, magnetic charge, mirrors, anti-de Sitter
boundaries, bound states, and complex-frequency quasinormal boundary conditions.
A scalar mass parameter $\mu\ge0$, with units $\mathrm m^{-1}$, would change
the asymptotic propagating wave number (when $\omega>\mu$) to
$\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$ and require a different scattering normalization.
The real-frequency Wronskian identity makes no claim about complex-frequency
mode problems with other boundary conditions.

statement.before: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a nondegenerate alternating bilinear form $\\omega:V\\times V\\to\\mathbb R$. For a linear subspace $W\\subseteq V$, define $W^\\omega:=\\{v\\in V:\\omega(v,w)=0\\text{ for every }w\\in W\\}$, and assume $W^\\omega\\subseteq W$ (so $W$ is coisotropic). Then the quotient vector space $W/W^\\omega$, whose elements are cosets $[u]:=u+W^\\omega$, carries the well-defined symplectic form $\\overline\\omega([u],[v])=\\omega(u,v)$. This proposition concerns only finite-dimensional constrained mode models; it does not assert that an infinite-dimensional Einstein–Maxwell solution space has a smooth symplectic quotient.
