Adopt the following classical test-scalar model in the geometric length-coordinate convention of the charged radial-scattering definition. Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|\le M$, put

$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad U:=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2.$$

On $U$ prescribe

$$g=-f(r)\,dt^2+f(r)^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad F=dA=-\frac{Q}{r^2}\,dt\wedge dr.$$

Here $\gamma_{S^2}$ is the unit round metric, $A_t\to0$ at infinity, and $r_+$ is the larger positive root; in the extremal case $Q^2=M^2$ both roots equal $M$. The factorization $f(r)=(r-r_+)(r-r_-)/r^2$ makes $f>0$ on this open exterior. For horizon terminology only, use the selected ingoing RN metric $g_{\mathrm{in}}=-f(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}$ on $\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2$. The hypersurface $H_+:=\{r=r_+\}$ is a null Killing horizon for $\xi:=\partial_v$: $g_{\mathrm{in}}^{-1}(dr,dr)=f(r_+)=0$, $\mathcal L_\xi g_{\mathrm{in}}=0$, and $\xi$ is everywhere nonzero and tangent to $H_+$; moreover $\xi^\flat=dr$ on $H_+$, so $\xi$ is null and normal there and its nonzero-generator part is all of $H_+$. This local statement asserts no global causal-boundary property of a maximal spacetime extension. Orient the product by $dt\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$, where $\omega_{S^2}$ is the outward area form of the unit round sphere; $\star_g$ denotes the corresponding Lorentzian Hodge map. Adopt the source-free background Maxwell branch $dF=0$ and $d(\star_gF)=0$ on $U$. The fields are prescribed on the open exterior only. No maximal spacetime extension, continuation of the scalar field or its equation across the horizon, coupled Einstein equation, or actual astrophysical object is asserted by this postulate.

In the chosen global electric gauge, let $\psi:U\to\mathbb C$ be a smooth complex scalar and let $e\in\mathbb R$ be its fixed charge-coupling parameter. Define $D_a\psi:=\partial_a\psi-ieA_a\psi$, so $D_t=\partial_t+ieQ/r$. The scalar Laplace–Beltrami operator on the unit sphere is $\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}=\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta)+\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\phi^2$ in the standard polar chart, with smooth global extension. Adopt the massless, minimally coupled equation

$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi=0.$$

For its energy bookkeeping, adopt the symmetric tensor assignment $\mathsf T_{ab}[\psi;g,A,e]$ defined by the exact mathematical stress-tensor formula linked below. The scalar's stress is omitted from the equations for the prescribed background, and no scalar source is added to its Maxwell equation. This is a test-field model: omission of the scalar response is a modeling choice, not an estimate that the response is small.

Coordinates $t,r,M,Q$ have unit metres; $f$ and $A_t$ are dimensionless; $e$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$; $F_{tr}$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$; and the scalar field has a specified but otherwise arbitrary unit $[\psi]$. The tensor assignment $\mathsf T_{ab}$ has component unit $[\psi]^2\mathrm m^{-2}$ in this geometric normalization. For the subextremal branch, define the gauge-normalized outer-root potential difference by $\Phi_H:=A_t(\infty)-A_t(r_+)=Q/r_+$. The separate mathematical scalar model on the Einstein–Maxwell page uses SI bookkeeping and its own coupling parameters; no identification with those parameters is made here.

Let $E:[0,T_{\max})\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, let $E_0\ge0$, $C>0$, $\epsilon>0$ and $\delta>0$ be dimensionless, and suppose for every finite $t<T_{\max}$ that

$$E(t)\le E_0+C\epsilon\int_0^t(1+s)^{-1-\delta}E(s)\,ds.$$

Use the dimensionless thresholds $A,\epsilon,\eta$ in the cited continuation contract, with $2A\epsilon^2<\eta$. Then

$E(t)\le E_0\exp\!\left(\frac{C\epsilon}{\delta}\left[1-(1+t)^{-\delta}\right]\right)\le E_0e^{C\epsilon/\delta}.$$

Use the positive dimensionless thresholds $A$, $\epsilon$ and $\eta$ of the continuation contract below, with $2A\epsilon^2<\eta$. If $E_0e^{C\epsilon/\delta}<A\epsilon^2$, this scalar estimate gives the strict improvement required by that contract. It supplies no Einstein decay estimate; an application must prove this integral inequality and its continuation margins separately.

Use the dimensionless angular coordinates $x^i$ and the periodic spatial
three-torus from the earlier fixed-gauge data definition. Choose integers
$N_i\ge3$, coordinate spacings $\Delta_i:=2\pi/N_i$, and the finite periodic
grid
$$
G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=\{(2\pi j_1/N_1,2\pi j_2/N_2,2\pi j_3/N_3): 0\le j_i<N_i\}\subset\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}.
$$
At each grid node $p$, supply a real symmetric positive-definite matrix
$h_{ij}(p)$ and its matrix inverse $h^{ij}(p)$ (so
$h^{ik}(p)h_{kj}(p)=\delta^i{}_j$), a real symmetric array $K_{ij}(p)$,
a scalar $\rho(p)$, a covector array $j_i(p)$, and real constants $\Lambda$
and $\kappa>0$. These are the sampled spatial metric, second fundamental
form, energy density and momentum density in the convention of
[[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]]: for a future unit normal $n$
and the coordinate basis $\partial_i$, $K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_Xn,Y)$,
$\rho=T(n,n)$ and $j_i=-T(n,\partial_i)$, where $T$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant two-tensor. The array definition itself needs only the listed
samples and does not assume the continuum field equation. The vacuum case is
$\rho=j_i=\Lambda=0$. In the SI angular-coordinate convention used here,
$[x^i]=1$, $[h_{ij}]=\mathrm m^2$, $[K_{ij}]=\mathrm m$,
$[\rho]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, $[j_i]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}$,
$[\Lambda]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and
$[\kappa]=\mathrm{m^{-1}\,kg^{-1}\,s^2}$. Thus the scalar residual below
has units $\mathrm m^{-2}$ and its covector components in this angular basis
have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

Let $\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}$ denote the real arrays indexed by
the grid. Choose and specify linear maps
$\delta_i:\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}\to
\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}$ with $\delta_i1=0$; apply them
componentwise to tensor arrays. Periodic index wrapping is used here. Define
the discrete connection components, curvature, Ricci array and scalar
curvature by nodewise operations, with every index $i,j,k,\ell,a,b$ ranging
over $1,2,3$ and repeated upper/lower indices summed:
$$
\Gamma^k{}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}:= \frac12h^{k\ell}(\delta_i h_{j\ell}+\delta_j h_{i\ell}-\delta_\ell h_{ij}),
$$
$$
R^a{}_{b i j,\boldsymbol\Delta}:= \delta_i\Gamma^a{}_{jb,\boldsymbol\Delta} -\delta_j\Gamma^a{}_{ib,\boldsymbol\Delta} +\Gamma^a{}_{i\ell,\boldsymbol\Delta}\Gamma^\ell{}_{jb,\boldsymbol\Delta} -\Gamma^a{}_{j\ell,\boldsymbol\Delta}\Gamma^\ell{}_{ib,\boldsymbol\Delta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}:=R^k{}_{i k j,\boldsymbol\Delta}, \qquad R_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}.
$$
Set
$$
\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ij}K_{ij},\qquad |K|^2_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell},
$$
$$
(D_i^{\boldsymbol\Delta}K)_{kj}:= \delta_iK_{kj}-\Gamma^\ell{}_{ik,\boldsymbol\Delta}K_{\ell j} -\Gamma^\ell{}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}K_{k\ell}.
$$
The signed discrete Hamiltonian and momentum residuals are
$$
\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:= R_{\boldsymbol\Delta}+\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}^2 -|K|^2_{\boldsymbol\Delta}-2\Lambda-2\kappa\rho,
$$
$$
\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta,j}:= h^{ik}(D_i^{\boldsymbol\Delta}K)_{kj} -\delta_j\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}+\kappa j_j.
$$
These signs match the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints in
[[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]] when its pointwise equation
$G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$ is assumed. The displayed discrete formulas are array
operations: they do not define a coordinate-covariant discrete connection or
assume a discrete Leibniz rule. A reconstruction map has the exact type
$$
\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:\mathcal D_{\boldsymbol\Delta}\longrightarrow \mathcal C,
$$
where $\mathcal D_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$ is the set of all grid arrays
$(h_{ij},K_{ij},\rho,j_i)$ with the pointwise symmetry and positive-definite
conditions above, and $\mathcal C$ is the set of pointwise assignments on
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ of a positive-definite symmetric covariant two-tensor
$h$, a symmetric covariant two-tensor $K$, a scalar $\rho$ and a covector
$j$, with the same units. No continuity or differentiability of a member of
$\mathcal C$ is implied; if continuum derivatives are used, the needed
regularity must be stated separately. Specify $\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$
as part of each diagnostic, since it records which continuum field the grid
is intended to represent. For every reported diagnostic, also record the grid
norm and its weights, the mesh hierarchy, the units, the derivative maps, the
periodic boundary treatment, and $\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$. A small
residual by itself does not assert closeness to an exact constraint-satisfying
development.

Let $N\ge4$ be even, let $N_2,N_3\ge3$, let $L_*>0$ be a length, and choose
$0<\varepsilon<1$. On $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ with dimensionless angular
coordinates $x^i$, set
$$
\widetilde h=L_*^2\bigl((dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2\bigr),\qquad \widetilde\sigma=0,\qquad \tau=0,\qquad \phi_N(x)=1+\varepsilon\sin(Nx^1/2).
$$
Take the vacuum branch with $\Lambda=0$ and $\rho=j=0$, so the conformal data
are $h=\phi_N^4\widetilde h$ and $K=0$. Use a periodic mesh with
$N_1=N$ and counts $N_2,N_3$ in the other directions. Put
$\Delta_i=2\pi/N_i$ and use nodes
$x^i_{j_i}=2\pi j_i/N_i$, $0\le j_i<N_i$, with indices wrapped modulo each
$N_i$. For $i=1,2,3$, let $\mathbf e_i$ be the $i$th standard basis vector of
$\mathbb Z^3$. For a scalar grid array
$f_{\mathbf j}$, use the centered periodic maps
$$
(\delta_i f)_{\mathbf j}:= \frac{f_{\mathbf j+\mathbf e_i}-f_{\mathbf j-\mathbf e_i}}{2\Delta_i}, \qquad i=1,2,3,
$$
with indices reduced modulo $(N_1,N_2,N_3)$, and apply them componentwise.
For reconstruction, partition each periodic coordinate circle into the
half-open cells
$$
C_{\mathbf j}:=\prod_{i=1}^3 \left[\frac{2\pi(j_i-1/2)}{N_i}, \frac{2\pi(j_i+1/2)}{N_i}\right)\pmod{2\pi},
$$
and assign every component on $C_{\mathbf j}$ its value at node
$\mathbf j$. This specifies the piecewise-constant map
$\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$ in the constraint-residual definition.
For the reported residual arrays use uniform dimensionless weights
$w_{\mathbf j}:=(NN_2N_3)^{-1}$ and the norm
$$
\| (\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta},\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta})\|_{\boldsymbol\Delta,2} :=\left(\sum_{\mathbf j}w_{\mathbf j} \left(|\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta}(\mathbf j)|^2+ h^{ik}(\mathbf j)\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta,i}(\mathbf j) \mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta,k}(\mathbf j)\right)\right)^{1/2}.
$$
The bars around the scalar residual denote the real absolute value. For the
sampled scalar and covector arrays, define the bilinear form
$$
\langle (H,M),(\widehat H,\widehat M)\rangle_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=\sum_{\mathbf j}w_{\mathbf j}\left(H(\mathbf j)\widehat H(\mathbf j)+h^{ik}(\mathbf j)M_i(\mathbf j)\widehat M_k(\mathbf j)\right).
$$
At the nodes of this example $h^{ik}=L_*^{-2}\delta^{ik}$ and every
$w_{\mathbf j}=(NN_2N_3)^{-1}$ is positive. Hence this bilinear form is
positive definite on the finite-dimensional space of scalar and covector
grid arrays, and the displayed quantity is its induced norm. In the fixed SI
component convention, each summand has units $\mathrm m^{-4}$, so the norm has
units $\mathrm m^{-2}$.
This example reports one mesh only, with no refinement hierarchy or
convergence comparison.

The discrete residuals $\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$ and
$\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$ vanish at every grid node, so their stated
weighted norm is zero. However, the
continuum Hamiltonian residual at $x^1=\pi/N$ is
$$
\mathcal H(h,K)=\frac{2\varepsilon N^2}{L_*^2(1+\varepsilon)^5}>0.
$$
Thus a smooth high-frequency field can have the same samples and zero discrete
residual as flat data while violating the continuum constraint between grid
points. A small or vanishing grid residual alone does not certify continuum
constraint satisfaction or solution accuracy.

statement.before:
Let $M$ be an oriented smooth four-manifold and let $\phi$ be a field
configuration in a specified smooth field bundle. A **local Lagrangian
four-form** $\mathcal L(\phi)$ is a smooth four-form whose coordinate
coefficients depend smoothly on the field components and finitely many
spacetime derivatives at each point. A **chosen first-variation
decomposition** consists of a linear Euler functional $E_\phi[\eta]$ with

Let $\mathcal L$ have a chosen first-variation decomposition with Euler
functional $E_\phi$. If $E_\phi=0$ and both variations satisfy the
linearized equations, so $\delta_iE_\phi=0$, then $d_M\omega=0$. For a finite
oriented smooth singular four-chain $C$ with
$\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$, where the $\Sigma_i$ are oriented
three-chains and $B$ is the remaining oriented boundary chain,

$$\Omega_{\Sigma_2}-\Omega_{\Sigma_1}=-\int_B\omega.$$

Thus on-shell closure alone gives independence between cuts only when the
side flux vanishes.

$\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$, where the $\Sigma_i$ are oriented
three-chains and $B$ is the remaining oriented boundary chain,

$$\Omega_{\Sigma_2}-\Omega_{\Sigma_1}=-\int_B\omega.$$

For a fixed smooth two-parameter family of commuting variations, replace the
Lagrangian and its selected potential by

$$\mathcal L'=\mathcal L+d_M\mu,\qquad \theta'(\phi;\delta\phi) =\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)+\delta\mu(\phi;\delta\phi) +d_MY(\phi;\delta\phi),$$

$$\omega'-\omega =d_M\bigl(\delta_2Y(\delta_1\phi)-\delta_1Y(\delta_2\phi)\bigr).$$

statement.before:
Let $M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $(X^1,X^2,X^3,X^4)=(t,x,y,z)$,
orientation $dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$, and flat metric
$-dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$. For one-forms use
$$*dt=-dx\wedge dy\wedge dz,\qquad *dx=-dt\wedge dy\wedge dz,\qquad *dy=dt\wedge dx\wedge dz,\qquad *dz=-dt\wedge dx\wedge dy.$$
Here the massless wave equation means
$(-\partial_t^2+\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2+\partial_z^2)u=0$. Let
$u_1:=t^2+x^2$ and $u_2:=t$, and define the smooth field family
$\psi_{a,b}:=a u_1+b u_2$ on $P=\mathbb R^2$. Both $u_1,u_2$ solve the
massless wave equation, so $\psi=0$ at $(a,b)=(0,0)$ is a solution and
$\delta_1\psi:=\partial_a\psi_{a,b}=u_1$,
$\delta_2\psi:=\partial_b\psi_{a,b}=u_2$ are commuting variations solving
that same equation.
Use the massless scalar Lagrangian
$\mathcal L=-\tfrac12d\psi\wedge*d\psi$, with selected potential
$\theta(\psi;\delta\psi)=-\delta\psi*d\psi$ and current
$\omega(\delta_1,\delta_2)
=\delta_2\psi*d\delta_1\psi-\delta_1\psi*d\delta_2\psi$.
For $0<t_1<t_2$ and $L>0$, put
$a_0=(t_1,0,0,0)$ and
$(\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4)=(t_2-t_1,L,1,1)$. Let
$$T_4:=\{r\in\mathbb R^4:r_j\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_{j=1}^4r_j\le1\}$$
with orientation $dr_1\wedge dr_2\wedge dr_3\wedge dr_4$. For each
permutation $\rho\in S_4$, define vertices
$$v_0^\rho:=a_0,\qquad v_j^\rho:=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^j\ell_{\rho(k)}e_{\rho(k)}\quad(1\le j\le4),$$
where $e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4$ is the standard basis in the ordered coordinates
$(t,x,y,z)$. Define the 24 affine simplex maps and their oriented sum by
$$\sigma_\rho(r):=v_0^\rho+\sum_{j=1}^4r_j(v_j^\rho-v_0^\rho),\qquad
C:=\sum_{\rho\in S_4}\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\,\sigma_\rho.$$
Each map has domain orientation $dr_1\wedge dr_2\wedge dr_3\wedge dr_4$;
the coefficient $\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)$ orients it relative to
$dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$.

For $t\in\{t_1,t_2\}$, let $b_t=(t,0,0,0)$ and
$(m_1,m_2,m_3)=(L,1,1)$. With
$$T_3:=\{r\in\mathbb R^3:r_j\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_{j=1}^3r_j\le1\}$$
oriented by $dr_1\wedge dr_2\wedge dr_3$, define, for $\rho\in S_3$,
$$w_0^{t,\rho}:=b_t,\qquad
w_j^{t,\rho}:=b_t+\sum_{k=1}^jm_{\rho(k)}\widehat e_{\rho(k)}\quad(1\le j\le3),$$
where $\widehat e_1=e_2$, $\widehat e_2=e_3$, and $\widehat e_3=e_4$, and put
$$\sigma_{t,\rho}(r):=w_0^{t,\rho}+\sum_{j=1}^3r_j(w_j^{t,\rho}-w_0^{t,\rho}),\qquad
\Sigma_t:=\sum_{\rho\in S_3}\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\,\sigma_{t,\rho}.$$
Each $\Sigma_t$ is oriented by $dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$. Define the side chain
by $B:=\partial C-\Sigma_{t_2}+\Sigma_{t_1}$, with the signed simplex-face
multiplicities inherited from the boundary of $C$. The coordinate-order
boundary calculation shows that $B$ is supported on the six side faces of the
box, each with outward-normal-first orientation from
$dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$; their
oriented volume forms are $+dt\wedge dy\wedge dz$ at $x=0$,
$-dt\wedge dy\wedge dz$ at $x=L$,
$-dt\wedge dx\wedge dz$ at $y=0$,
$+dt\wedge dx\wedge dz$ at $y=1$,
$+dt\wedge dx\wedge dy$ at $z=0$, and
$-dt\wedge dx\wedge dy$ at $z=1$. Then the bulk current is
closed on the box, and by definition of $B$,
$\partial C=\Sigma_{t_2}-\Sigma_{t_1}+B$, but
$$\Omega_{\Sigma_{t_2}}-\Omega_{\Sigma_{t_1}} =-L(t_2^2-t_1^2)\ne0.$$
The oriented side flux is $L(t_2^2-t_1^2)$, so the finite-region balance is
$\Omega_{\Sigma_{t_2}}-\Omega_{\Sigma_{t_1}}=-\int_B\omega$. The box is
compact; the example uses no asymptotic region or falloff premise.

statement.before:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad
\omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad
F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,
$F$ is the local curvature two-form of $\nabla$. A local $\Lambda$ is a
change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

statement.before:
On $M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, metric
$g=-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2$, and Cartesian coframe
$e=(dx^0,dx^1,dx^2,dx^3)^{\mathsf T}$, set
$\theta(x)=x^1$ and let

$$\Lambda(x)=\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&0\\
0&\cos\theta&-\sin\theta&0\\
0&\sin\theta&\cos\theta&0\\
0&0&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.$$

The changed coframe $e'=\Lambda e$ has the same metric, and its connection
matrix
$\omega'=-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}=-Jd\theta$, where
$J^1{}_2=-1$, $J^2{}_1=1$ and all other entries vanish, is nonzero while
its curvature is zero. This is a pure-gauge local Lorentz connection. The
rotation has the local spin lift
$A(x)=\exp(-i\theta(x)\sigma_3/2)\in SL(2,\mathbb C)$.

statement.before:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H_0,\mathcal H$ be separable complex Hilbert spaces, $H_0$ and $H$ self-adjoint operators on them, and $J:\mathcal H_0\to\mathcal H$ a bounded linear map. Write $E_{H_0}$ and $E_H$ for their spectral projection valued measures. The absolutely continuous subspace $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$ consists of vectors $u$ for which the scalar measure $B\mapsto\|E_{H_0}(B)u\|^2$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure; $P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$ is its orthogonal projection. Define the two-space wave operators, when the pointwise strong limits exist on $\mathcal H_0$, by

$$\Omega_\pm(H,H_0;J):=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty} e^{itH}J e^{-itH_0}P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0),$$

where a strong limit means that for every $u\in\mathcal H_0$ the vector-valued expression converges in $\mathcal H$. The two signs are separate limits. When $J=I$ and $\mathcal H_0=\mathcal H$, write $\Omega_\pm(H,H_0)$. A wave operator is complete when its range is all of $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$. When both wave operators exist and are isometries on $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$, the scattering operator on that subspace is

$$S(H,H_0;J):=\Omega_+^*\Omega_-.$$

When both are complete with common range $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$, $S$ is unitary. For a fixed finite number $r\ge1$ of channels on an open energy interval $I\subset\mathbb R$, finite-channel data additionally consists of the standard space $\mathbb C^r$ and a matrix field $S:I\to U(r)$, where

$$U(r):=\{U\in M_r(\mathbb C):U^*U=UU^*=I_r\}.$$

Here $U^*$ is conjugate transpose, $\operatorname{tr}U=\sum_{j=1}^r U_{jj}$, and $\det U$ is the usual alternating determinant. The fixed channel number means that $I$ contains no channel threshold. This finite-channel data is an explicit on-shell input; the abstract wave-operator definition alone does not assert that a given pair has finite-dimensional energy fibers.

statement.before: Assuming AC, a nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system on a finite-dimensional real symplectic space with fixed nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger system; regularity, finite phase space, irreducibility, and the nonzero parameter are necessary hypotheses.
statement.proposed:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\in\mathbb N_0$, let $V$ be a real vector space of dimension $2n$, and let $\omega:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be bilinear and alternating, meaning $\omega(v,v)=0$ for every $v\in V$, and nondegenerate, meaning that $\omega(v,w)=0$ for every $w\in V$ implies $v=0$. Let $\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space. A unitary operator on $\mathcal H$ means a bijective complex-linear isometry. Suppose $W:V\to U(\mathcal H)$ satisfies $W(0)=I$ and

$$W(v)W(w)=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}W(v+w)\qquad(v,w\in V),$$

is regular in the sense that $t\mapsto W(tv)\xi$ is norm-continuous for every $v\in V$ and $\xi\in\mathcal H$, and is irreducible in the sense that its only closed subspaces $M\subseteq\mathcal H$ satisfying $W(v)M\subseteq M$ for every $v\in V$ are $\{0\}$ and $\mathcal H$. Choose a symplectic basis identifying $(V,\omega)$ with $\mathbb R^n\oplus\mathbb R^n$ and $\omega((q,p),(q',p'))=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$. Then $W$ is unitarily equivalent, meaning that there is a unitary map $U:\mathcal H\to L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ intertwining the two Weyl actions, to the Schrödinger system

$$\bigl(W_\lambda(q,p)f\bigr)(x)=e^{i\lambda p\cdot(x-q/2)}f(x-q)$$

on $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$. Consequently, there is exactly one unitary-equivalence class of nonzero irreducible regular Weyl systems with this fixed finite-dimensional phase space and parameter. No conclusion is asserted for infinite-dimensional phase spaces, nonregular systems, or zero central parameter.

statement.before:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $SU(2)=\{W\in M_2(\mathbb C):W^*W=I,\det W=1\}$, and let $\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. For $i\in\{x,y,z\}$ put $A_i(t)=\cos(t/2)I-i\sin(t/2)\sigma_i$. Let $V\ne\{0\}$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and let $D:SU(2)\to U(V)$ be a differentiable unitary representation. Define its self-adjoint infinitesimal generators $J_i$ by $\frac{d}{dt}D(A_i(t))|_{t=0}=-iJ_i$. For complex-linear maps $X,Y:V\to V$, write $[X,Y]:=XY-YX$. Assume $[J_x,J_y]=iJ_z$, $[J_y,J_z]=iJ_x$, and $[J_z,J_x]=iJ_y$, and that the triple is irreducible, meaning that no nonzero proper subspace $M\subset V$ satisfies $J_iM\subseteq M$ for all $i$. The spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\ldots\}$ is its largest $J_z$ eigenvalue, as in the finite spin-block classification. Then

$$D(-I)=(-1)^{2s}I_V.$$

Let $\rho:SU(2)\to SO(3)$ be the standard two-sheeted covering homomorphism with kernel $\{I,-I\}$. Give $PU(V)=U(V)/\{zI:|z|=1\}$ its quotient topology and let $q:U(V)\to PU(V)$ be the quotient map; write $[U]:=q(U)$. The ray action $R\mapsto[D(W)]$ for any lift $W$ of $R$ is a well-defined continuous homomorphism $SO(3)\to PU(V)$. For integer $s$, $D$ itself descends to an ordinary unitary representation of $SO(3)$; for half-integer $s$, its unitary representation does not descend, while its ray representation does. No classification of all projective representations of $SO(3)$ is asserted.

The projective descent is summarized by the following commutative diagram; $q$ is the quotient map $U(V)\to PU(V)$ and $\overline D$ is the ray representation just defined.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}
SU(2) \arrow[r,"D"] \arrow[d,"\rho"'] & U(V) \arrow[d,"q"]\\
SO(3) \arrow[r,"\overline D"'] & PU(V)
\end{tikzcd}
```

The proof below verifies that $q\circ D$ is constant on each $\rho$-fiber, which defines $\overline D$ and makes this diagram commute; no proof step relies on the diagram.

statement.proposed:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal H=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\mathcal H_j$ be a finite orthogonal direct sum of nonzero complex Hilbert spaces, with $r\ge1$, and let $P_j$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H_j$. Write $\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ for the algebra of bounded linear operators on $\mathcal H$. Let $\mathcal A$ be the block-diagonal subalgebra

$$\mathcal A=\left\{A\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H):A=\sum_{j=1}^rP_jAP_j\right\}.$$

For every trace-class operator $\rho$ on $\mathcal H$, define $\mathcal E(\rho)=\sum_{j=1}^rP_j\rho P_j$. Then, for every $A\in\mathcal A$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho A)=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal E(\rho)A).$$

Thus $\rho$ and $\mathcal E(\rho)$ define the same trace functional on the specified block-diagonal algebra. This is relative to the declared algebra; it implies no universal superselection law for a larger observable algebra.

Let $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$, $J$ and $W(z)$ have the
interleaved conventions of the definition. Define the real permutation
matrix $\Pi$ by
$$\Pi(x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_r,y_r)^T=(x_1,\ldots,x_r,y_1,\ldots,y_r)^T,$$
and, writing $Q=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r)^T$ and $P=(P_1,\ldots,P_r)^T$, set

$$S_g=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}(U+V)&-\operatorname{Im}(U-V)\\ \operatorname{Im}(U+V)&\operatorname{Re}(U-V)\end{pmatrix}$$

unitary, such that $M^*aM=a'$ and $M^*R_gM=S_gR_g$ on the transported

$$M^*W_g(w)M=W_g(S_g^Tw)\qquad(w\in\mathbb R^{2r}).$$

statement.proposed:
Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space whose inner product is linear in its first argument. Let $Q\subseteq H$ be a dense linear subspace, and let $q:Q\times Q\to\mathbb C$ be a Hermitian sesquilinear form: it is linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear in its second, and $q(u,v)=\overline{q(v,u)}$ for all $u,v\in Q$. In particular, $q(u,u)\in\mathbb R$. Write $q[u]=q(u,u)$. Assume $q[u]\ge-c\|u\|^2$ for some real $c\ge0$, and assume $Q$ is complete in the form norm $\|u\|_{q,c}^2=q[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$; this is the meaning of a closed semibounded form here.

For an integer $n\ge1$, let $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n\in Q$ be linearly independent. The exact input matrices are the Gram matrix $G$ and form matrix $A$ with entries

$$G_{ij}=\langle\phi_j,\phi_i\rangle,\qquad A_{ij}=q(\phi_j,\phi_i)\qquad(1\le i,j\le n).$$

For every nonzero coefficient vector $z\in\mathbb C^n$, $z^*Gz=\|\sum_jz_j\phi_j\|^2>0$, so $G$ is positive definite; the symmetry of $q$ makes $A$ Hermitian.

The procedure is:

1. Form $G$ and $A$ from the supplied vectors and form, using exact entries.
2. Diagonalize the positive definite Hermitian matrix $G$ and form its unique positive inverse square root $G^{-1/2}$. Set $B=G^{-1/2}AG^{-1/2}$.
3. Diagonalize the Hermitian matrix $B$, listing its real eigenvalues $\rho_1\le\cdots\le\rho_n$ with multiplicity and selecting an orthonormal eigenbasis $y_1,\ldots,y_n$. For each $j$, set $c_j=G^{-1/2}y_j$ and return $(\rho_j,c_j)$.

Repeated eigenvalues may return any orthonormal basis of the corresponding eigenspace. The procedure uses trial vectors in $Q$ and does not require them to lie in the operator domain of an associated self-adjoint operator. It operates on exact matrix entries: if quadrature or an approximate eigensolver supplies numerical data, this procedure alone supplies no error enclosure or certification for those approximations.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space, let $A=A^*$ satisfy $A\ge-cI$ for some $c\ge0$, and set $Q(A)=D((A+cI)^{1/2})$. Define the associated closed form by

$$q_A(u,v)=\langle(A+cI)^{1/2}u,(A+cI)^{1/2}v\rangle-c\langle u,v\rangle\qquad(u,v\in Q(A)).$$

Let $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ be the essential spectrum, the complement in $\sigma(A)$ of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, and put $\alpha=\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, with $\alpha=+\infty$ when this set is empty. For $k\ge1$, define

$$\lambda_k(A)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq Q(A)\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u],\qquad q_A[u]=q_A(u,u),$$

where the infimum over an empty family is $+\infty$. For a finite-dimensional conforming subspace $V\subseteq Q(A)$ and $1\le k\le\dim V$, define its $k$th Ritz value

$$\theta_k(V)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq V\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u].$$

Then $\theta_k(V)\ge\lambda_k(A)$. If $V_1\subseteq V_2\subseteq\cdots\subseteq Q(A)$ are finite-dimensional subspaces whose union is dense in $Q(A)$ in the form norm $\|u\|_{Q(A)}^2=q_A[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$, then for every fixed $k$ with $\lambda_k(A)<\alpha$ the values $\theta_k(V_n)$, defined once $\dim V_n\ge k$, decrease to $\lambda_k(A)$, the $k$th isolated eigenvalue below the essential spectrum counted with multiplicity.

statement.proposed:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space, let $T=T^*$ be self-adjoint on $H$, and fix $\hbar>0$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $t_0\in I$, and let $v\in C^1(I;H)$ satisfy $v(s)\in D(T)$ for every $s\in I$ and $s\mapsto Tv(s)$ continuous. Define $r(s)=i\hbar v'(s)-Tv(s)$ and $U_T(t,t_0)=e^{-i(t-t_0)T/\hbar}$ by the Borel functional calculus. Then for every $t\in I$,

$$\|v(t)-U_T(t,t_0)v(t_0)\|\le\frac1\hbar\int_{\min(t,t_0)}^{\max(t,t_0)}\|r(s)\|\,ds.$$

The integral is the ordinary integral of the continuous real-valued function $s\mapsto\|r(s)\|$; the bound is conditional on the stated operator-domain regularity and makes no assertion about an asymptotic approximation outside this residual estimate.

Fix a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a finite index set $A$ with real basis $\{t^a\}_{a\in A}$, and a finite species index set $I$. Let $\mathfrak g_{\mathbb C}:=\mathfrak g\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ be the complexification of [[def-complexification-of-a-real-lie-algebra]], with complex scalar multiplication on the second tensor factor and the complex-bilinear bracket specified on pure tensors by $[X\otimes z,Y\otimes w]=[X,Y]\otimes zw$ for $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C$. Identify $X\in\mathfrak g$ with its canonical real embedding $X\otimes1$; in particular $t^a$ in a representation argument means $t^a\otimes1$. For each $i\in I$, let $V_i$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $\rho_i:\mathfrak g_{\mathbb C}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_i)$ be a complex-linear Lie-algebra representation, so $\rho_i([U,V])=\rho_i(U)\rho_i(V)-\rho_i(V)\rho_i(U)$. Attach the bookkeeping label $\chi_i=L$ to each species. In this interface, a “left-handed Weyl species” means exactly the data $(V_i,\rho_i,\chi_i=L)$; the label is not a spinor field or a chirality operator. No spacetime manifold, spinor bundle or field, kinetic operator or action, integration of $\rho_i$ to a gauge group, regulator, effective action, or gauge-variation map is constructed or assumed.

Set $T^a_{R_i}:=\rho_i(t^a)$ and define $\{A,B\}:=AB+BA$ for endomorphisms of $V_i$. The algebraic cubic representation coefficient is
$$d^{abc}=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}\!\left(T^a_{R_i}\{T^b_{R_i},T^c_{R_i}\}\right)\in\mathbb C.$$
The basis and generator normalization are fixed as part of the data. No factor $1/2$ is included in the anticommutator. If $T^{(b}T^{c)}=(T^bT^c+T^cT^b)/2$, then $d^{abc}$ is twice $\sum_i\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}(T^a_{R_i}T^{(b}_{R_i}T^{c)}_{R_i})$. Cancellation of this coefficient means $d^{abc}=0$ for every basis triple in this convention. These are representation traces only; calling them anomaly coefficients in a physical model requires an additional theorem.

Define the separate linear representation coefficient by
$$\ell^a=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}(T^a_{R_i})\in\mathbb C.$$
For one-dimensional representation spaces of a one-dimensional Abelian Lie algebra with fixed generator $t$ and $\rho_i(t)=q_i\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C}$, this gives $\ell=\sum_iq_i$. The coefficient $\ell^a$ is recorded separately because a later mixed gauge-gravitational analysis needs its own representation data. Such an analysis must specify its spacetime and gauge connections, curvature conventions, and index polynomial; no mixed-anomaly formula is asserted by this interface.

The only local BRST obstruction statement recorded here is a separate formal result for the specific Abelian jet complex used by the mathematical supplier, not a BRST construction for the general Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ above. In the convention of `def-qftx-brst-relative-local-cohomology`, a compactly supported local horizontal $p$-form is a finite sum of $f_{i_1\ldots i_p}(x,z)\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_p}$, with each coefficient smooth and compactly supported in $x\in\mathbb R^4$ and polynomial in finitely many field-jet coordinates $z^i_\alpha$; $i$ indexes the field and ghost generators and $\alpha$ their derivative multi-indices. Its total derivative is $D_\mu=\partial/\partial x^\mu+\sum_{i,\alpha}z^i_{\alpha+e_\mu}\partial_L/\partial z^i_\alpha$, where $e_\mu$ is the unit multi-index and $\partial_L$ is the left graded derivative; $d_H=dx^\mu\wedge D_\mu$. The differential $s$ is the odd ghost-number-one Abelian derivation fixed by `def-qftx-abelian-local-brst`, with $sa_\mu=\partial_\mu c_{\mathrm{gh}}$, $sc_{\mathrm{gh}}=0$, $s\bar c=B$, $sB=0$, and $s\psi=igc_{\mathrm{gh}}\psi$, extended by the graded Leibniz rule and commutation with spacetime derivatives; $a_\mu,\psi,B$ are even, $c_{\mathrm{gh}},\bar c$ are odd, and their ghost numbers are $0,0,0,1,-1$, respectively. This source also fixes $s^2=d_H^2=0$ and $sd_H+d_Hs=0$, with nilpotence of $s$ established by `lem-qftx-brst-nilpotence-doublets`. For each $n$, $\mathcal K_n^{r,p}$ is an $s,d_H$-stable subcomplex of these forms, and the relative class is the quotient
$$H^{1,4}(s|d_H;\mathcal K_n)=\frac{\{a_4\in\mathcal K_n^{1,4}:s a_4+d_Ha_3=0\text{ for some }a_3\in\mathcal K_n^{2,3}\}}{\{s b_4+d_Hc_3:b_4\in\mathcal K_n^{0,4},\ c_3\in\mathcal K_n^{1,3}\}}.$$
The direct supplier `prop-qftx-anomaly-obstruction` is a draft proposition with a supplied conditional proof. Its scalar construction premise is the draft theorem `thm-qftx-scalar-eg-induction`: under the Axiom of Choice (every family of nonempty sets has a choice function) and Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function), and for admissible flat scalar free data and a local scalar polynomial class as defined by `def-qftx-local-time-ordered-system`, that theorem asserts existence of symmetric multilinear time-ordered maps satisfying its contract at every finite order, with finite graph scaling bounds and local extension ambiguities. It asserts no convergence, adiabatic limit, positivity, or Ward identity. The exact statement of `prop-qftx-anomaly-obstruction` assumes those data and a time-ordering scheme satisfying that theorem. For each ghost number $r$, define the local-functional quotient $\mathscr F_n^r:=\mathcal K_n^{r,4}/d_H\mathcal K_n^{r,3}$ and its formal series module $\mathscr F_n^r\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$, where $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate. For some $n\ge1$, it further assumes an odd formal ghost-number-one operator $\mathcal W_\hbar=s+\sum_{j\ge1}\hbar^j\mathcal W_j$ on this module, $\mathcal W_\hbar^2=0$, and an element $X\in\mathscr F_n^0\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$ with $\mathcal W_\hbar X=\hbar^n\mathcal A+O(\hbar^{n+1})$, where $O(\hbar^{n+1})$ denotes terms of formal degree at least $n+1$, all lower coefficients vanish, and $\mathcal A=[a_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ for compactly supported $a_4\in\mathcal K_n^{1,4}$. It requires $\mathcal K_n^{0,4}$ to be exactly the admissible local counterterm densities. Under these hypotheses, that proposition states that $s a_4$ is $d_H$-exact and that shifting $X$ by $-\hbar^n[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$, for $b_4\in\mathcal K_n^{0,4}$, cancels the order-$n$ breaking exactly when $[a_4]_{s|d_H}=0$. This is used only in the stated conditional form: it does not establish that the hypotheses hold for the representation data above or construct a physical effective action, and it does not prove a quantum action principle.

Accordingly, this interface asserts no physical anomaly-cancellation criterion from $d^{abc}$. A later physical theorem must specify its spacetime, field space, action, regulator and renormalized effective-action map, and the map that assigns a local gauge-variation density to that data. It must then prove the relation of that density to an explicitly specified local BRST cohomology class and invariant six-form polynomial, with mixed gauge-gravitational coefficients and loop-order hypotheses stated separately. No conclusion about transformations outside the identity component of a separately specified full gauge-transformation group follows from this infinitesimal representation tensor. Vanishing $d^{abc}$ alone proves neither a nonperturbative gauge theory nor the absence of failures under such transformations.

Fix a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a finite index set $A$ with real basis $\{t^a\}_{a\in A}$, and a finite species index set $I$. Let $\mathfrak g_{\mathbb C}:=\mathfrak g\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ be the complexification of [[def-complexification-of-a-real-lie-algebra]], with complex scalar multiplication on the second tensor factor and the complex-bilinear bracket specified on pure tensors by $[X\otimes z,Y\otimes w]=[X,Y]\otimes zw$ for $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C$. Identify $X\in\mathfrak g$ with its canonical real embedding $X\otimes1$; in particular $t^a$ in a representation argument means $t^a\otimes1$. For each $i\in I$, let $V_i$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $\rho_i:\mathfrak g_{\mathbb C}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_i)$ be a complex-linear Lie-algebra representation, so $\rho_i([U,V])=\rho_i(U)\rho_i(V)-\rho_i(V)\rho_i(U)$. Attach the bookkeeping label $\chi_i=L$ to each species. In this interface, a “left-handed Weyl species” means exactly the data $(V_i,\rho_i,\chi_i=L)$; the label is not a spinor field or a chirality operator. No spacetime manifold, spinor bundle or field, kinetic operator or action, integration of $\rho_i$ to a gauge group, regulator, effective action, or gauge-variation map is constructed or assumed.

Set $T^a_{R_i}:=\rho_i(t^a)$ and define $\{A,B\}:=AB+BA$ for endomorphisms of $V_i$. The algebraic cubic representation coefficient is
$$d^{abc}=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}\!\left(T^a_{R_i}\{T^b_{R_i},T^c_{R_i}\}\right)\in\mathbb C.$$
The basis and generator normalization are fixed as part of the data. No factor $1/2$ is included in the anticommutator. If $T^{(b}T^{c)}=(T^bT^c+T^cT^b)/2$, then $d^{abc}$ is twice $\sum_i\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}(T^a_{R_i}T^{(b}_{R_i}T^{c)}_{R_i})$. Cancellation of this coefficient means $d^{abc}=0$ for every basis triple in this convention. These are representation traces only; calling them anomaly coefficients in a physical model requires an additional theorem.

Define the separate linear representation coefficient by
$$\ell^a=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}(T^a_{R_i})\in\mathbb C.$$
For one-dimensional representation spaces of a one-dimensional Abelian Lie algebra with fixed generator $t$ and $\rho_i(t)=q_i\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C}$, this gives $\ell=\sum_iq_i$. The coefficient $\ell^a$ is recorded separately because a later mixed gauge-gravitational analysis needs its own representation data. Such an analysis must specify its spacetime and gauge connections, curvature conventions, and index polynomial; no mixed-anomaly formula is asserted by this interface.

The only local BRST obstruction statement recorded here is a separate formal result for the specific Abelian jet complex used by the mathematical supplier, not a BRST construction for the general Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ above. In the convention of `def-qftx-brst-relative-local-cohomology`, a compactly supported local horizontal $p$-form is a finite sum of $f_{i_1\ldots i_p}(x,z)\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_p}$, with each coefficient smooth and compactly supported in $x\in\mathbb R^4$ and polynomial in finitely many field-jet coordinates $z^i_\alpha$; $i$ indexes the field and ghost generators and $\alpha$ their derivative multi-indices. Its total derivative is $D_\mu=\partial/\partial x^\mu+\sum_{i,\alpha}z^i_{\alpha+e_\mu}\partial_L/\partial z^i_\alpha$, where $e_\mu$ is the unit multi-index and $\partial_L$ is the left graded derivative; $d_H=dx^\mu\wedge D_\mu$. The differential $s$ is the odd ghost-number-one Abelian derivation fixed by `def-qftx-abelian-local-brst`, with $sa_\mu=\partial_\mu c_{\mathrm{gh}}$, $sc_{\mathrm{gh}}=0$, $s\bar c=B$, $sB=0$, and $s\psi=igc_{\mathrm{gh}}\psi$, extended by the graded Leibniz rule and commutation with spacetime derivatives; $a_\mu,\psi,B$ are even, $c_{\mathrm{gh}},\bar c$ are odd, and their ghost numbers are $0,0,0,1,-1$, respectively. This source also fixes $s^2=d_H^2=0$ and $sd_H+d_Hs=0$, with nilpotence of $s$ established by `lem-qftx-brst-nilpotence-doublets`. For each $n$, $\mathcal K_n^{r,p}$ is an $s,d_H$-stable subcomplex of these forms, and the relative class is the quotient
$$H^{1,4}(s|d_H;\mathcal K_n)=\frac{\{a_4\in\mathcal K_n^{1,4}:s a_4+d_Ha_3=0\text{ for some }a_3\in\mathcal K_n^{2,3}\}}{\{s b_4+d_Hc_3:b_4\in\mathcal K_n^{0,4},\ c_3\in\mathcal K_n^{1,3}\}}.$$
The direct supplier `prop-qftx-anomaly-obstruction` is a draft proposition with a supplied conditional proof. Its scalar construction premise is the draft theorem `thm-qftx-scalar-eg-induction`: under the Axiom of Choice (every family of nonempty sets has a choice function) and Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function), and for admissible flat scalar free data and a local scalar polynomial class as defined by `def-qftx-local-time-ordered-system`, that theorem asserts existence of symmetric multilinear time-ordered maps satisfying its contract at every finite order, with finite graph scaling bounds and local extension ambiguities. It asserts no convergence, adiabatic limit, positivity, or Ward identity. The exact statement of `prop-qftx-anomaly-obstruction` assumes those data and a time-ordering scheme satisfying that theorem. For each ghost number $r$, define the local-functional quotient $\mathscr F_n^r:=\mathcal K_n^{r,4}/d_H\mathcal K_n^{r,3}$ and its formal series module $\mathscr F_n^r\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$, where $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate. For some $n\ge1$, it further assumes an odd formal ghost-number-one operator $\mathcal W_\hbar=s+\sum_{j\ge1}\hbar^j\mathcal W_j$ on this module, $\mathcal W_\hbar^2=0$, and an element $X\in\mathscr F_n^0\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$ with $\mathcal W_\hbar X=\hbar^n\mathcal A+O(\hbar^{n+1})$, where $O(\hbar^{n+1})$ denotes terms of formal degree at least $n+1$, all lower coefficients vanish, and $\mathcal A=[a_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ for compactly supported $a_4\in\mathcal K_n^{1,4}$. It requires $\mathcal K_n^{0,4}$ to be exactly the admissible local counterterm densities. Under these hypotheses, that proposition states that $s a_4$ is $d_H$-exact and that there exists an admissible $b_4\in\mathcal K_n^{0,4}$ such that shifting $X$ by $-\hbar^n[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ cancels the order-$n$ breaking if and only if $[a_4]_{s|d_H}=0$. This is used only in the stated conditional form: it does not establish that the hypotheses hold for the representation data above or construct a physical effective action, and it does not prove a quantum action principle.

Accordingly, this interface asserts no physical anomaly-cancellation criterion from $d^{abc}$. A later physical theorem must specify its spacetime, field space, action, regulator and renormalized effective-action map, and the map that assigns a local gauge-variation density to that data. It must then prove the relation of that density to an explicitly specified local BRST cohomology class and invariant six-form polynomial, with mixed gauge-gravitational coefficients and loop-order hypotheses stated separately. No conclusion about transformations outside the identity component of a separately specified full gauge-transformation group follows from this infinitesimal representation tensor. Vanishing $d^{abc}$ alone proves neither a nonperturbative gauge theory nor the absence of failures under such transformations.

statement.before:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of
nonempty sets admits a function $s$ with $s(n)\in X_n$ for every $n$.
Use the following SI constants and meanings: $c>0$ is the speed of light in
vacuum, in m s$^{-1}$; $\hbar>0$ is the reduced Planck constant, in J s;
$e>0$ is the magnitude of the elementary charge, in C; and $\mu_0>0$ is the
vacuum permeability, in H m$^{-1}$, used here as a positive parameter without
assigning it a numerical value. Set
$$g=e\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}>0,$$
which is dimensionless. These are the adopted QFT SI conventions.

Let $I$ be a finite, possibly empty, set of leg labels. For each $i\in I$,
choose an energy $E_i>0$ in J and a physical velocity
$\mathbf v_{i,\mathrm{phys}}\in\mathbb R^3$ in m s$^{-1}$ with
$|\mathbf v_{i,\mathrm{phys}}|<c$. Write
$v_i=\mathbf v_{i,\mathrm{phys}}/c\in\mathbb R^3$, so $v_i$ is
dimensionless and $|v_i|<1$. Also choose a dimensionless charge number
$Q_i\in\mathbb R$ (the assigned physical charge is $eQ_i$ in C) and an
orientation $\eta_i\in\{-1,1\}$, where $-1$ denotes an incoming leg and
$+1$ an outgoing leg. Assume charge balance
$\sum_{i\in I}\eta_iQ_i=0$. For four-vectors
$a=(a^0,\mathbf a),b=(b^0,\mathbf b)\in\mathbb R^4$, write
$h=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$ and
$h(a,b)=a^0b^0-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b$ for the algebraic contraction
with signature $(+,-,-,-)$ used in this model.

For $n\in S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and angular frequency
$\nu>0$ in s$^{-1}$, with associated model photon energy $\hbar\nu$ in J,
put $p_i=E_i(1,v_i)$ and $q=\hbar\nu(1,n)$ in $\mathbb R^4$. On
$$\mathscr Q=\{\hbar\nu(1,n):\nu>0,\ n\in S^2\}\subset\mathbb R^4,$$
define the prescribed current $J:\mathscr Q\to\mathbb R^4$ and angular
coefficient $K:S^2\to\mathbb R^4$ by
$$J(q)=\sum_{i\in I}\eta_iQ_i\frac{p_i}{h(p_i,q)},\qquad K(n)=\sum_{i\in I}\eta_iQ_i\frac{(1,v_i)}{1-v_i\cdot n}.$$
Because $|v_i\cdot n|\le |v_i|<1$, every denominator
$1-v_i\cdot n$ is strictly positive.
The data make $h(p_i,q)=E_i\hbar\nu(1-v_i\cdot n)>0$ and
$J(q)=K(n)/(\hbar\nu)$. The balance condition gives
$h(J(q),q)=0$; this is the conservation convention for this prescribed
eikonal current in the model. Here “prescribed eikonal current” means exactly
the displayed rational map $J$ on these model photon energy four-vectors; no
scattering-amplitude factorization or approximation is asserted.

Let $A\subseteq S^2$ be a Borel angular acceptance region. The sphere
$S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$ is a compact embedded smooth hypersurface, and
$d\Omega$ denotes its Euclidean chart surface measure: for a finite regular
injective $C^1$ chart cover $X_j:V_j\to S^2$, where each $V_j$ is open in
$\mathbb R^2$, with $C^1$ coordinate
transitions and a subordinate ambient partition of unity $\chi_j$ whose supports are compactly
contained in the chart neighborhoods, its integral on a nonnegative Borel
function $F$ is
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\Omega=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_jF)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy.$$
This is the chart-independent induced surface integral. Write
$K(n)=(K^0(n),\mathbf K(n))$ and define
$K_\perp(n)=(I_3-nn^T)\mathbf K(n)$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$
identity matrix. Put
$$b_0(n)=\frac{gK_\perp(n)}{\sqrt{2(2\pi)^3}},\qquad b(n)=\mathbf1_A(n)b_0(n),\qquad C=\int_{S^2}|b(n)|^2\,d\Omega(n).$$
The earlier current theorem proves $b_0\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$
for these finite balanced subluminal legs; since $A$ is Borel,
$b\in L^2$ and $0\le C\le\int_{S^2}|b_0|^2d\Omega<\infty$.
Thus $b$ and $C$ are dimensionless.

For the one-particle space, write
$$x\cdot y=\sum_{j=1}^3x_jy_j\quad(x,y\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j\quad(a,b\in\mathbb C^3),$$
where the second dot product is the complex-bilinear extension. The fiber
Hermitian pairing is $\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline{a_j}b_j$, with
norm $|a|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$. Set
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
Here $d^3\mathbf k$ is Lebesgue measure, and this pairing is
second-variable-linear. For $\mathbf k\ne0$,
put $\widehat{\mathbf k}=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$
and $P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\widehat{\mathbf k}\widehat{\mathbf k}^{T}$, the
Euclidean orthogonal projection onto the fiber plane perpendicular to
$\mathbf k$; assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$. Its multiplier is an
orthogonal projection on $\mathcal H$, so its range is closed. The transverse
one-particle Hilbert space
is
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T}=\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for a.e. }\mathbf k\ne0\},$$
where $M_{P_T}$ is multiplication by $P_T$, and the real Euclidean dot
product is extended complex-bilinearly in the transverse condition. This is
the transverse one-particle space used in this model.

For $m\ge1$, use the iterated Hilbert tensor completion
$\mathcal H_T^{\widehat\otimes m}$, with product pairing on elementary
tensors. Here $S_m$ is the permutation group and
$U_\pi(u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_m)=
u_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{\pi^{-1}(m)}$. Set
$$P_{s,m}=\frac1{m!}\sum_{\pi\in S_m}U_\pi,\qquad \mathcal H_s^{(m)}=\operatorname{Ran}P_{s,m};$$
put $P_{s,0}=I_{\mathbb C}$ and $\mathcal H_s^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. The
symmetric bosonic Fock space is
$$\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)=\left\{(\Psi_m)_{m\ge0}:\Psi_m\in\mathcal H_s^{(m)},\ \sum_{m\ge0}\|\Psi_m\|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with componentwise pairing and vacuum $1\in\mathbb C$ in sector zero.
For $f\in\mathcal H_T$, define the exponential-vector map
$\epsilon:\mathcal H_T\to\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$ by
$$\epsilon(f)=\bigoplus_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{P_{s,m}(f^{\otimes m})}{\sqrt{m!}}.$$
Here $f^{\otimes0}=1$ in the vacuum sector.
Since $f^{\otimes m}$ is already symmetric,
$P_{s,m}(f^{\otimes m})=f^{\otimes m}$ for $m\ge1$; write this tensor as
$f^{\otimes_s m}$.

For fixed angular-frequency cutoffs $0<\varepsilon<\Delta<\Lambda$, let
$\nu(\mathbf k)=c|\mathbf k|$ in s$^{-1}$, with $\mathbf k$ in m$^{-1}$.
The one-particle coherent displacement is the transverse mode function
$$f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}(\mathbf k)= \mathbf1_{\{\varepsilon<\nu(\mathbf k)<\Lambda\}}|\mathbf k|^{-3/2} {}\times b\!\left(\frac{\mathbf k}{|\mathbf k|}\right) \quad(\mathbf k\ne0), \qquad f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}(0)=0.$$
The function $f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}$ has units m$^{3/2}$ in
$\mathcal H_T$; the associated free one-photon energy is
$\hbar\nu(\mathbf k)=\hbar c|\mathbf k|$ in J. Define its normalized
coherent vector by
$$\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}\|^2}{2}\right)\epsilon(f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}).$$
For a finite partition
$B_1,\ldots,B_r$ of $(\varepsilon,\Lambda)$ into disjoint Borel intervals,
let
$H_j=\{u\in\mathcal H_T:u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ a.e. unless }\nu(\mathbf k)\in B_j\}$.
These are pairwise orthogonal closed subspaces because the intervals are
disjoint.
For a tuple $(m_1,\ldots,m_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, put $M=\sum_jm_j$.
Its occupation subspace is the closed span in sector $\mathcal H_s^{(M)}$
of the vectors
$$P_{s,M}\left(\bigotimes_{j=1}^r\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^{m_j}u_{j,\ell}\right),\qquad u_{j,\ell}\in H_j,$$
where the empty tensor for $M=0$ is the vacuum $1\in\mathbb C$. It has
exactly $m_j$ factors in $H_j$ and no factor outside $\bigoplus_jH_j$.
Define $N(B_j)$ to have value $m_j$ on this subspace.
The model assigns the tuple
probability equal to the squared norm of the projection of
$\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}$ onto it. Its resolution parameter
$\Delta$ divides $(\varepsilon,\Lambda)$ into the unresolved band
$(\varepsilon,\Delta)$ and the resolved band $[\Delta,\Lambda)$. The
threshold frequency is assigned to the resolved band; its exact assignment
does not change any $L^2$ vector or probability because a single frequency
has zero one-particle measure.
This is a finite-cutoff free coherent-state model; it does not posit a
detector response or an interacting QED scattering law.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and a constant $\hbar>0$, interpreted as the angular-momentum scale. Let $M=\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\mathbf n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$, and use the transverse one-photon Hilbert space
$$
\mathcal H_T^\nu=\{f\in L^2(M,d\nu;\mathbb C^3):\mathbf k\cdot f(\mathbf k)=0\ \nu\text{-almost everywhere}\},\qquad d\nu(\mathbf k)=\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{2|\mathbf k|},
$$
with the second-variable-linear Hermitian pairing of [[def-qftx-photon-helicity-bundle]]. Use its dense smooth transverse domain
$$
\mathcal D=\{f\in C_c^\infty(M;\mathbb C^3):\mathbf k\cdot f(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for every }\mathbf k\in M\}.
$$
For $\mathbf n\in S^2$, let $P(\mathbf n)=I-\mathbf n\mathbf n^T$ and $h(\mathbf n)=i(\mathbf n\times\cdot)$, where the cross product is extended complex-linearly and $\epsilon_{123}=1$. These are the transverse projection and helicity multiplier from [[def-qftx-photon-helicity-bundle]]; on $P(\mathbf n)\mathbb C^3$, $h$ is self-adjoint, $h^2=P$, and its eigenvalues are $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$.

Let $e_1,e_2,e_3$ be the standard basis and define the dimensionless spin-one matrices by
$$
(S_i v)_a=-i\sum_{b=1}^3\epsilon_{iab}v_b,\qquad i,a\in\{1,2,3\}.
$$
Let $J_i$ be the self-adjoint Stone generator of the rotation subgroup about $e_i$ supplied by [[thm-qftx-photon-rotations-helicity]], with convention $U(R_{e_i}(t))=e^{-itJ_i/\hbar}$. Define the bounded projected spin operator and its orbital remainder by
$$
S_i'=M_{\hbar P(\mathbf n)S_iP(\mathbf n)}=M_{\hbar n_i h(\mathbf n)},\qquad L_i'=J_i-S_i'\quad\text{on the exact domain }D(J_i).
$$
Here $M_Af(\mathbf k)=A(\mathbf n(\mathbf k))f(\mathbf k)$ for a matrix field $A$; the proof below establishes the equality of the two formulas for $S_i'$, boundedness, self-adjointness, and invariance of $\mathcal D$. The label “projected spin” denotes this operator family and does not assert that its components form a spin-$1$ representation.

statement.proposed:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, $\hbar>0$, and the bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T^\nu)$ of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. For $R\in SO(3)$ define the Fock rotation by
$$
\Gamma(U(R))=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}U(R)^{\otimes_s n},
$$
where the vacuum sector $n=0$ carries the identity. This is a strongly continuous unitary representation. For a unit axis $\mathbf a$, its Stone generator $J_{\mathbf a}^{\mathrm F}$ is self-adjoint on its exact Stone domain and on finite symmetric tensors with factors in $D(J_{\mathbf a})$ acts as the sector sum
$$
d\Gamma(J_{\mathbf a})=\sum_{r=1}^{n} I^{\otimes(r-1)}\otimes J_{\mathbf a}\otimes I^{\otimes(n-r)}.
$$
In this statement $d\Gamma(J_{\mathbf a})$ denotes that Stone generator; the formula specifies its action on the stated finite-particle domain.

Let $\mathscr D_{\rm fin}(\mathcal D)$ be the vacuum plus the finite linear span of symmetrized elementary tensors whose one-particle factors lie in $\mathcal D$. It is a dense invariant domain, and on it the Fock total generators satisfy $[J_i^{\mathrm F},J_j^{\mathrm F}]=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}J_k^{\mathrm F}$.

For helicity $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$, define $N_\sigma$ on the $n$-particle sector by
$$
N_\sigma^{(n)}=\sum_{r=1}^n I^{\otimes(r-1)}\otimes P_\sigma\otimes I^{\otimes(n-r)}
$$
and use its maximal direct-sum domain $\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_n\|N_\sigma^{(n)}\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$. Define the helicity-number difference $D_h=d\Gamma(h)$ as the self-adjoint sector multiplier with $n$-particle action $\sum_{r=1}^n h^{(r)}$ and exact domain
$$
D(D_h)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}\left\|\sum_{r=1}^n h^{(r)}\Psi_n\right\|^2<\infty\right\};
$$
the vacuum term is zero. On finite-particle vectors $D_h=N_+-N_-$. With the natural-unit free radial phase
$$
(V_t f)(\mathbf k)=e^{-it|\mathbf k|}f(\mathbf k),\qquad t\in\mathbb R,
$$
the Fock lift $\Gamma(V_t)$ commutes with $D_h$, so the helicity-number difference is conserved by this free isotropic propagation. If $f\in\mathcal H_T^\nu$ is a normalized one-photon helicity-$\sigma$ vector, meaning $\|f\|_\nu=1$ and $P_\sigma f=f$ almost everywhere, then
$$\langle f,S_z'f\rangle_\nu=\hbar\sigma\int_M\cos\theta(\mathbf k)\,|f(\mathbf k)|^2\,d\nu(\mathbf k),\qquad \theta(\mathbf k)=\arccos\!\left(\frac{k_z}{|\mathbf k|}\right)\in[0,\pi].$$
When $|\mathbf k|$ has inverse-length units, $t$ has length units in this $c=1$ convention. These are mathematical consequences of the specified one-photon and Fock models, not claims about a measured field or apparatus.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a complex modular ribbon fusion category with finite simple-label set $I$, unit label $0$, simple pivotal dimensions $d_i$, twists $\theta_i$, and Hopf-link matrix $s$. Choose a square root $D\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ of $\sum_{i\in I}d_i^2$ and set $S=s/D$, $p_+=\sum_{i\in I}\theta_i d_i^2$, and $\kappa=p_+/D$. Modularity means that $s$ is invertible; no positivity of $d_i$ or $D$ is assumed.

Use the weighted Lagrangian ribbon-bordism category whose objects are closed oriented marked surfaces with a Lagrangian in real first homology and whose morphisms are compact oriented three-bordisms with colored ribbon graphs and integer weights. For composable bordisms $M_1:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$ and $M_2:\Sigma_1\to\Sigma_2$, let $R_1,R_2$ be their individual homology Lagrangian relations and let $R^t$ denote relation transpose. In the specified middle surface, set $K_1=R_1(\lambda_0)$, $K_0=\lambda_1$, and $K_2=R_2^t(\lambda_2)$; composition assigns weight $n_2+n_1+\mu(K_1,K_0,K_2)$, with the Walker signature/Maslov sign and order. For a genus-$g$ surface with ordered labels $W_1,\ldots,W_n$, write $H=\bigoplus_{i\in I}i\otimes i^*$ and

$$V(\Sigma;W_1,\ldots,W_n)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf 1,W_1\otimes\cdots\otimes W_n\otimes H^{\otimes g}).$$

The weighted RT model is this category, these finite-dimensional complex state spaces, and the exact surgery-defined symmetric monoidal functor $Z$ of the supplied theorem. It includes actual coupon morphisms, disconnected bordisms and empty ends; increasing an integer weight by one multiplies the map by $\kappa$. The model retains the full anomaly and asserts no ordinary anomaly-free functor unless cancellation data are supplied separately.

statement.proposed:
A **finite groupoid** is a small category in which every morphism is invertible, with finitely many isomorphism classes and a finite automorphism group at every object. Write $\pi_0(\mathcal C)$ for its set of isomorphism classes. Its **groupoid cardinality** is

$$|\mathcal C|:=\sum_{[c]\in\pi_0(\mathcal C)}\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(c)|}.$$

For an isomorphism-invariant function $f:\pi_0(\mathcal C)\to\mathbb C$, define

$$\int_{c\in\mathcal C} f(c):=\sum_{[c]\in\pi_0(\mathcal C)}\frac{f(c)}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(c)|}.$$

For finite groupoids $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$, a functor $p:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$, and an object $d$ of $\mathcal D$, its **homotopy fiber** $\mathcal C_d$ has objects $(c,\alpha)$ with $\alpha:p(c)\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}d$ and morphisms $u:(c,\alpha)\to(c',\alpha')$ satisfying $\alpha'\circ p(u)=\alpha$. Define pullback and pushforward of invariant functions by

$$(p^*g)([c])=g([p(c)]),\qquad (p_!f)([d])=\int_{(c,\alpha)\in\mathcal C_d} f([c]).$$

A span $\mathcal X\xleftarrow{a}\mathcal E\xrightarrow{b}\mathcal Y$ of finite groupoids therefore induces the linear map $b_!a^*$ on invariant functions.

Let $p:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ and $q:\mathcal E\to\mathcal D$ be functors of finite groupoids. The **homotopy pullback groupoid** $\mathcal C\times^h_{\mathcal D}\mathcal E$ has objects $(c,e,\alpha)$, where $c\in\mathcal C$, $e\in\mathcal E$, and $\alpha:p(c)\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}q(e)$ is an isomorphism in $\mathcal D$. statement.proposed:
Let $K$ be a finite connected CW complex and $G$ a finite group. Choose an orientation of each 1-cell and, for each 2-cell, its based attaching word in the finite edge presentation of $\pi_1(K)$; the choice of base paths is part of that presentation. A **flat edge assignment** is a label $g_e\in G$ for every oriented 1-cell with $g_{\bar e}=g_e^{-1}$, such that each attaching word has holonomy $1$. If a word traverses edges $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ in that order with exponents $\epsilon_j\in\{1,-1\}$, its holonomy is $g_{e_m}^{\epsilon_m}\cdots g_{e_1}^{\epsilon_1}$.

Write $\operatorname{Flat}(K,G)$ for the finite set of flat assignments and $K_0$ for the vertices. The finite vertex gauge group $G^{K_0}$ acts by

$$(h\cdot g)_e=h_{t(e)}g_eh_{s(e)}^{-1},$$

where $s(e)$ and $t(e)$ are the source and target vertices. The **finite flat connection groupoid** $\mathcal C_G(K)$ is the action groupoid $\operatorname{Flat}(K,G)//G^{K_0}$: its objects are flat assignments and its arrows $g\to g'$ are the $h\in G^{K_0}$ with $h\cdot g=g'$. Its untwisted finite BF partition function is the groupoid cardinality

$$Z_G(K):=|\mathcal C_G(K)|=\sum_{[g]\in\operatorname{Flat}(K,G)/G^{K_0}}\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Stab}(g)|} =\frac{|\operatorname{Flat}(K,G)|}{|G|^{|K_0|}}.$$

This is a finite combinatorial model; it has no continuous Lie-algebra-valued connection integral or additional cocycle phase.

For a finite disconnected CW complex, define $\mathcal C_G(K)$ to be the product of the groupoids of its connected components; for the empty complex use the terminal groupoid.

Let $p:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ and $q:\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z$ be functors of finite groupoids. The iterated homotopy fiber over any $z\in\mathcal Z$ is equivalent to the homotopy fiber of $q\circ p$, so $(q\circ p)_!=q_!p_!$. statement.proposed:
Work in one named laboratory chart with spatial coordinate space $\mathbb R^3$ and time coordinate $t\in\mathbb R$. Let $q\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ be the framework charge parameter, let $m>0$ be an externally supplied mass parameter, and take the SI constants $c>0$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$ of the electromagnetic framework. Define the positive time constant

$$\tau:=\frac{q^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0mc^3}>0.$$

The units are $[q]=\mathrm C$, $[m]=\mathrm{kg}$, $[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $[\varepsilon_0]=\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$, so $[\tau]=\mathrm s$. A prescribed external force is a continuous map $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ with units $\mathrm N$. A particle trajectory in this model is a map $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ with three continuous time derivatives; its velocity and acceleration are $v(t):=\dot x(t)$ and $a(t):=\ddot x(t)$, with units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The term point particle means that the model assigns one position $x(t)$ and no spatial extent.

Adopt, as an additional effective model postulate, the equation

$$m\bigl(a(t)-\tau\dot a(t)\bigr)=f(t)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

Both $ma$ and $m\tau\dot a$ have units of force. The dot on $a$ means differentiation with respect to the laboratory time. This equation is not obtained by evaluating the particle's singular Maxwell self-field in the adopted Lorentz force law. The previously developed prescribed-source radiation model does not define that self-interaction; this postulate introduces a separate effective equation.

For physical use on a compact interval $I\subset\mathbb R$, assume $f$ is continuously differentiable there, choose dimensionless tolerances $\eta,\delta\in(0,1)$ and a positive force scale $F_*$ with units $\mathrm N$, and state the chosen values. In this item, low-speed at tolerance $\eta$ means $\sup_{t\in I}|v(t)|\le\eta c$, and slowly varying relative to $\tau$ at tolerance $\delta$ means $\tau\sup_{t\in I}|\dot f(t)|\le\delta F_*$. These are explicit regime conventions for an application, not universal empirical thresholds. The ODE is an exact adopted equation on its mathematical domain; its physical interpretation is restricted to applications that state their regime and tolerances.

statement.proposed:
Use the equation and constants of the preceding postulate, with $m,\tau>0$. Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and continuous, and let a solution mean a continuously differentiable map $a:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $m(a-\tau\dot a)=f$ at every real time. Bounded for a vector map means each of its three real coordinates is bounded; in $\mathbb R^3$ this is equivalent to bounded Euclidean norm. The vector improper Riemann integral below is taken componentwise, with $\int_t^\infty h(s)\,ds:=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_t^R h(s)\,ds$ when that limit exists. Then the integral converges absolutely, and

$$a_*(t):=\frac{1}{m\tau}\int_t^\infty \exp\!\left(-\frac{s-t}{\tau}\right)f(s)\,ds$$

is a bounded solution. For any fixed $t_0\in\mathbb R$, every solution has the form

$$a(t)=a_*(t)+C\exp\!\left(\frac{t-t_0}{\tau}\right),\qquad C\in\mathbb R^3$$

Here $C$ is a constant acceleration vector with units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

The only solution bounded on a future half-line $[T,\infty)$, for any finite $T$, is $a_*$. A nonzero $C$ gives an exponentially growing acceleration branch, called a runaway branch in this item. Moreover, there is a bounded smooth force that vanishes for $t\le0$, is nonzero for some $t\in(0,1)$, and for which $a_*(t)\ne0$ for every $t<0$. Preacceleration means this nonzero acceleration before the force begins; it is a property of the selected ODE branch, not an observation about a physical particle.

statement.proposed:
Assume the equation and bounded-force hypotheses of the preceding theorem: $m,\tau>0$, $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ is bounded and twice continuously differentiable, and the unique bounded-future solution $a_*$ is used. Suppose

$$M_2:=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|f''(t)|<\infty.$$

Since $f$ has units $\mathrm N$ and $t$ has units $\mathrm s$, $M_2$ has units $\mathrm{N\,s^{-2}}$.

Define the first-order reduction-of-order approximation by

$$a_{\mathrm{RO}}(t):=\frac{f(t)+\tau f'(t)}{m}.$$

Its residual when substituted into the adopted equation is exactly

$$m\bigl(a_{\mathrm{RO}}(t)-\tau a_{\mathrm{RO}}'(t)\bigr)-f(t)=-\tau^2 f''(t).$$

On the bounded-future branch the acceleration error obeys

$$|a_*(t)-a_{\mathrm{RO}}(t)|\le\frac{\tau^2 M_2}{m}\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

The residual and bound are exact conditional statements about the prescribed-force ODE; they do not assert that a nonlinear self-consistent particle trajectory is approximated by $a_{\mathrm{RO}}$.

statement.proposed:
In the adopted equation, set $f=0$ and fix any $t_0\in\mathbb R$. For every constant acceleration vector $C\in\mathbb R^3$ with units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, the acceleration $a_C(t)=C\exp((t-t_0)/\tau)$ is a solution. For any fixed position $x_0$ and velocity $v_0$ at $t_0$, a trajectory with that acceleration is

$$x_C(t)=x_0+v_0(t-t_0)+C\tau^2\left(\exp((t-t_0)/\tau)-1-\frac{t-t_0}{\tau}\right).$$

Thus the same position and velocity at $t_0$ admit different acceleration branches; $C\ne0$ grows exponentially as $t\to\infty$. This does not establish that any physical charge follows such a trajectory.

statement.proposed:
A phasor coefficient at frequency $\omega\in\mathbb R$ is a complex vector $g_0=g_R+ig_I\in\mathbb C^3$, with $g_R,g_I\in\mathbb R^3$, representing a real map $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by the real-part representation

$$g(t)=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(g_0\exp(-i\omega t)\right)=g_R\cos(\omega t)+g_I\sin(\omega t).$$

At $\omega=0$ this representation determines only $g_R$. Adopt the canonical static convention $g_0=G+i0$ for the constant function $g(t)\equiv G\in\mathbb R^3$; in particular the static force below has $v=0$ and $f_0=u+i0$. Static acceleration phasors use the same convention.

Let $\omega\in\mathbb R$ and $f_0=u+iv\in\mathbb C^3$, with $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$. For any $z=u+iv\in\mathbb C^3$, define $|z|:=\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^3|u_j|^2+\sum_{j=1}^3|v_j|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$, the Euclidean norm of its six real coordinates. The force amplitude $f_0$ has units N, $\omega$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and acceleration phasors have units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Prescribe the real force

$$f(t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(f_0\exp(-i\omega t)\right),$$

where real part is taken componentwise. The bounded-future acceleration has complex phasor amplitude

$$a_{*,0}=\frac{f_0}{m(1+i\omega\tau)}.$$

The first-order reduction-of-order acceleration $a_{\mathrm{RO}}=(f+\tau f')/m$ has phasor amplitude $a_{\mathrm{RO},0}=f_0(1-i\omega\tau)/m$. For $f_0\ne0$, the absolute amplitude error relative to the force acceleration scale $|f_0|/m$ is

$$\frac{|a_{*,0}-a_{\mathrm{RO},0}|}{|f_0|/m}=\frac{(\omega\tau)^2}{\sqrt{1+(\omega\tau)^2}}.$$

For any chosen tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, this relative amplitude error is at most $\epsilon$ exactly when

$$|\omega\tau|\le\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon^2+\sqrt{\epsilon^4+4\epsilon^2}}{2}}.$$

Hence small error at a small prescribed tolerance requires small $|\omega\tau|$; no universal numerical cutoff or experimental frequency response is asserted.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with the metric $d_1(q,r):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}|q(a)-r(a)|$ and its induced topology, called the $\ell^1$ topology. This is a metric: symmetry, nonnegativity and separation follow coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows by summing $|q(a)-s(a)|\leq|q(a)-r(a)|+|r(a)-s(a)|$. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. By [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]], this mass assignment is normalized and is a probability law; explicitly, $\sum_{x^n\in\mathcal A^n}\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p(a)=1$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the probability measure on Borel subsets $B\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal A)$ that assigns mass
$$p_{n,\beta}\bigl(\{x^n\in\Omega_n:L_n(x^n)\in B\}\bigr).$$

For a real-valued function $f$ on a nonempty set $S$, define $\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x):=\{x\in S:f(x)=\inf_{y\in S}f(y)\}$ and $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in S}f(x):=\{x\in S:f(x)=\sup_{y\in S}f(y)\}$; either set is empty if the corresponding extremum is not attained. For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $A\subseteq\Omega_n$ and an event $E\subseteq\Omega_n$ with $p^{\otimes n}(E)>0$, define the conditional probability by $p^{\otimes n}(A\mid E):=p^{\otimes n}(A\cap E)/p^{\otimes n}(E)$. For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $(K,d_K)$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $(\mu_n)_{n\geq1}$ be Borel probability measures on $K$. Let $I:K\to[0,+\infty]$ be lower semicontinuous, meaning that $\{x\in K:I(x)>a\}$ is open for every real $a$, and not identically $+\infty$. Assume the speed-$n$ large-deviation bounds
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(G)\geq-\inf_{x\in G}I(x)\quad\text{for every open }G\subseteq K,$$
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(C)\leq-\inf_{x\in C}I(x)\quad\text{for every closed }C\subseteq K,$$
with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$ and $\ln0=-\infty$. Let $F:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and put
$$Z_n:=\int_K e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x),\qquad c:=\sup_{x\in K}\bigl(F(x)-I(x)\bigr).$$
For Borel $B\subseteq K$, define the normalized exponential tilt
$$\nu_n^F(B):=Z_n^{-1}\int_B e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x).$$
Here a good rate function is a lower semicontinuous map $J:K\to[0,+\infty]$ whose sublevel sets $\{x:J(x)\leq a\}$ are compact for every real $a$. Then $Z_n$ is finite and positive,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln Z_n=c,$$
and $(\nu_n^F)$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with the good rate function $I_F(x):=I(x)-F(x)+c$. Its zero set is precisely $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in K}(F(x)-I(x)):=\{x\in K:F(x)-I(x)=c\}$, with $F(x)-(+\infty):=-\infty$.

statement.proposed:
Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and nonempty, let $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$, and let $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, where $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ is the probability simplex with its $\ell^1$ topology. Let $L_n$ be the empirical probability vector of an $n$-word drawn from $p^{\otimes n}$, and use $D(q\|p)=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln(q(a)/p(a))$ with zero-mass terms omitted. For $\beta\in\mathbb R$, the canonical word law weights $x^n$ proportionally to $p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}$.

The canonical macrostate law of $L_n$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with rate
$$R_\beta(q)=D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)-m_\beta,\qquad m_\beta:=\min_{r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(r\|p)+\beta h(r)\bigr].$$
Thus its canonical equilibrium macrostate set is $\mathcal M_\beta=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)]$.

For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, let $d(u):=\min_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$, $s(u):=-d(u)$, and $\mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$. If there is a sequence $\delta_j\downarrow0$ for which
$$\inf_{|h(q)-u|<\delta_j}D(q\|p)=\inf_{|h(q)-u|\leq\delta_j}D(q\|p)\quad\text{for every }j,$$
then the iterated microcanonical shell limit exists and is
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}\!\left(|h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=s(u).$$
In the same iterated limit, for every open neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_u$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}p^{\otimes n}\!\left(L_n\notin U\mid |h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=0.$$
Finally,
$$h(\mathcal M_\beta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))}\bigl[s(v)-\beta v\bigr],$$
and a macrostate $q$ is canonical at $\beta$ exactly when $q\in\mathcal M_{h(q)}$ and $h(q)$ maximizes $s(v)-\beta v$. Equivalently, $u$ is a canonical energy at $\beta$ exactly when $v\mapsto s(u)+\beta(v-u)$ is an upper supporting affine function for $s$ on the whole energy range. An energy with no upper supporting line for any slope is not realized by a canonical ensemble.

This is a dimensionless mathematical model: $J$, $\beta$, $h$, and $\Phi_\beta$ are dimensionless, so $\beta J$ is dimensionless. The labels “coupling” and “inverse-temperature parameter” are conventional names here and do not assign physical units.

Let $\mathcal A=\{-1,+1\}$ with uniform reference law $p(\pm1)=1/2$. For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$ define its magnetization $m(q):=q(+1)-q(-1)\in[-1,1]$ and the mean-field energy density $h(q):=-Jm(q)^2/2$, where $J>0$. For inverse-temperature parameter $\beta\geq0$, the canonical macrostate variational objective from the finite-alphabet model is
$$\Phi_\beta(m):=\frac{1+m}{2}\ln(1+m)+\frac{1-m}{2}\ln(1-m)-\frac{\beta Jm^2}{2},\qquad -1\leq m\leq1,$$
where $0\ln0:=0$. This objective has the unique global minimizer $m=0$ when $\beta J\leq1$. When $\beta J>1$, its global minimizers are exactly $m=\pm m_\beta$, where $m_\beta\in(0,1)$ is the unique positive solution of
$$m=\tanh(\beta Jm),\qquad \tanh x:=\frac{\exp(2x)-1}{\exp(2x)+1}.$$

Take the binary alphabet $\mathcal A=\{1,0\}$ with uniform reference $p=(1/2,1/2)$ and continuous energy-density map $h(q)=q(1)^{1/4}$ on $\Delta(\mathcal A)$. With $H_2(x):=-x\ln x-(1-x)\ln(1-x)$ and $0\ln0:=0$, the constrained entropy from the finite-alphabet mean-field model is $s(u)=H_2(u^4)-\ln2$ for $0\leq u\leq1$. For $0<u\leq1/10$,
$$s''(u)=u^2\left[12\ln\frac{1-u^4}{u^4}-\frac{16}{1-u^4}\right]>0.$$
Each such energy lies in an interval of strict convexity and therefore has no affine upper supporting line of any slope. Consequently none of these microcanonical energies is realized by a canonical mean-field ensemble at any $\beta\in\mathbb R$.
